One kilometer equals 1000 meters.
One meter equals 100 centimeters.
One inch equals 2.54 centimeters.
One foot equals 12 inches.
One yard equals 3 feet.
One mile equals 5280 feet, or about 1.609 kilometers.
One kilogram equals 1000 grams, or about 2.205 pounds.
One pound equals 16 ounces, or about 453.6 grams.
One metric tonne equals 1000 kilograms.
One liter equals 1000 milliliters.
One US gallon equals about 3.785 liters.
One hour equals 60 minutes, and one minute equals 60 seconds.
One day equals 24 hours, or 1440 minutes.
One week equals 7 days, and a common year has 365 days.
A leap year has 366 days, with February 29 as the extra day.
Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius, which is 32 degrees Fahrenheit.
Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level, which is 212 degrees Fahrenheit.
To convert Celsius to Fahrenheit, multiply by 9/5 and add 32.
Zero degrees Kelvin (absolute zero) equals -273.15 degrees Celsius.
One byte equals 8 bits.
One kibibyte equals 1024 bytes; one kilobyte equals 1000 bytes.
One dozen equals 12 items; one gross equals 144 items.
One acre equals 43,560 square feet.
One hectare equals 10,000 square meters.
One nautical mile equals 1.852 kilometers.
One horsepower equals about 746 watts.
One calorie equals about 4.184 joules.
One light-year is about 9.46 trillion kilometers.
One astronomical unit is the average Earth-Sun distance, about 150 million kilometers.
Speed of sound in air at sea level is about 343 meters per second.
World War I began in 1914 and ended in 1918.
World War II began in 1939 and ended in 1945.
The United States Declaration of Independence was signed in 1776.
The French Revolution began in 1789.
The Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
The first Moon landing, Apollo 11, was in July 1969.
The Wright brothers made the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
The Titanic sank in April 1912.
The printing press was developed by Johannes Gutenberg around 1440.
Christopher Columbus reached the Americas in 1492.
The Magna Carta was sealed in 1215.
The Roman Empire in the West fell in 476 CE.
The Great Fire of London occurred in 1666.
The United Nations was founded in 1945.
The European Union's euro currency entered circulation in 2002.
The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.
The first transatlantic telegraph cable was completed in 1858.
Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928.
The structure of DNA was described by Watson and Crick in 1953.
The World Wide Web was proposed by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989.
The first iPhone was released in 2007.
The Chernobyl nuclear accident occurred in 1986.
The Suez Canal opened in 1869.
The Panama Canal opened in 1914.
The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889.
The Great Wall of China was largely built during the Ming dynasty (1368-1644).
The Gregorian calendar was introduced in 1582.
Slavery was abolished in the United States by the 13th Amendment in 1865.
Women gained the right to vote in the United States in 1920.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in 1948.
Light travels at about 299,792 kilometers per second in a vacuum.
The Earth orbits the Sun once every 365.25 days.
The Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours, causing day and night.
The Moon orbits the Earth roughly every 27.3 days.
Gravity on Earth accelerates falling objects at about 9.8 meters per second squared.
Water is made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, H2O.
Table salt is sodium chloride, NaCl.
The human body is roughly 60 percent water.
The adult human body has 206 bones.
The human heart has four chambers: two atria and two ventricles.
Normal human body temperature is about 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 Fahrenheit).
Adult humans have 32 teeth including wisdom teeth.
Red blood cells carry oxygen using the protein hemoglobin.
The brain and spinal cord make up the central nervous system.
Neurons transmit signals using electrical impulses and chemical neurotransmitters.
DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid and carries genetic information.
Humans normally have 23 pairs of chromosomes, 46 in total.
Photosynthesis converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen using sunlight.
Plants absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen.
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum; it needs a medium.
Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
The atomic nucleus contains protons and neutrons and holds nearly all of an atom's mass.
Protons carry positive charge, electrons negative, neutrons no charge.
The periodic table currently has 118 confirmed elements.
Diamond and graphite are both made purely of carbon.
The most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere is nitrogen, about 78 percent.
Oxygen makes up about 21 percent of Earth's atmosphere.
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14, with 7 being neutral.
Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature, where molecular motion is minimal.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed (conservation of energy).
The mitochondrion is the organelle that produces most of a cell's ATP energy.
Antibiotics treat bacterial infections, not viral ones.
Vaccines train the immune system to recognize pathogens.
The four classical states of matter are solid, liquid, gas, and plasma.
Copper and silver are excellent electrical conductors.
An electric current is a flow of electric charge, measured in amperes.
Voltage is measured in volts, resistance in ohms, power in watts.
Ohm's law states that voltage equals current times resistance.
The speed of a wave equals its frequency times its wavelength.
Isaac Newton formulated the three laws of motion.
The Pacific Ocean is the largest and deepest ocean on Earth.
The Atlantic Ocean is the second-largest ocean.
The Nile and the Amazon are the two longest rivers in the world.
Mount Everest, at 8,849 meters, is Earth's highest mountain above sea level.
The Mariana Trench contains the deepest known point in the ocean.
The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world.
Antarctica is the coldest continent and holds most of Earth's fresh water as ice.
Africa is the second-largest continent by land area, after Asia.
Australia is both a country and a continent.
The equator divides the Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
The Amazon rainforest is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth.
The Great Barrier Reef, off Australia, is the world's largest coral reef system.
Russia is the largest country in the world by land area.
Canada has the longest coastline of any country.
The Caspian Sea is the largest inland body of water.
Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest freshwater lake.
The Dead Sea shore is the lowest land elevation on Earth.
Greenland is the world's largest island that is not a continent.
The Himalayas contain most of the world's highest peaks.
The Andes is the longest continental mountain range, running along South America.
The Mississippi River flows into the Gulf of Mexico.
The Danube flows through more countries than any other river.
Tokyo is among the most populous metropolitan areas in the world.
The Strait of Gibraltar separates Europe from Africa.
The Panama Canal connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.
The Suez Canal connects the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea.
Earth's surface is about 71 percent water.
There are seven continents on Earth.
The Ring of Fire around the Pacific has most of Earth's active volcanoes.
The Gobi Desert spans northern China and southern Mongolia.
Pi is approximately 3.14159 and is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
The square root of 144 is 12.
A right angle measures 90 degrees.
The angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees.
The Pythagorean theorem states a squared plus b squared equals c squared for right triangles.
A prime number has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself.
The first five prime numbers are 2, 3, 5, 7, and 11.
Zero is neither positive nor negative.
Any number multiplied by zero equals zero.
The area of a circle is pi times the radius squared.
The circumference of a circle is 2 pi times the radius.
A hexagon has six sides; an octagon has eight.
Percent means per hundred: 25 percent equals one quarter.
The factorial of 5 is 120.
Two to the tenth power is 1024.
The Fibonacci sequence starts 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13.
An even number is divisible by 2 with no remainder.
The sum of the first n integers is n times (n+1) divided by 2.
A dozen is 12; a score is 20.
In Roman numerals, X is 10, L is 50, C is 100, D is 500, and M is 1000.
The Sun is a G-type main-sequence star at the center of our solar system.
There are eight planets in the solar system.
Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun; Neptune is the farthest.
Venus is the hottest planet due to its dense carbon dioxide atmosphere.
Mars is called the Red Planet because of iron oxide on its surface.
Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system.
Saturn is famous for its prominent ring system.
Earth is the third planet from the Sun.
The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite.
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun.
A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon.
The Milky Way is the galaxy that contains our solar system.
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
A comet's tail always points away from the Sun.
The International Space Station orbits Earth roughly every 90 minutes.
Neil Armstrong was the first human to walk on the Moon.
Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon.
Polaris, the North Star, sits nearly above Earth's North Pole.
Galaxies contain billions of stars held together by gravity.

macOS 15 is named Sequoia and was released in 2024.
macOS 14 is named Sonoma and was released in 2023.
macOS 13 is named Ventura and was released in 2022.
macOS 12 is named Monterey and was released in 2021.
macOS 11 is named Big Sur and was the first version to run on Apple silicon (2020).
macOS 10.15 is named Catalina and was the last version to support 32-bit apps (it dropped them).
The macOS kernel is named XNU and its Unix layer is certified UNIX 03.
Apple silicon Macs use ARM64 (AArch64) processors; earlier Macs used Intel x86-64.
Rosetta 2 translates Intel x86-64 apps to run on Apple silicon Macs.
The default macOS file system is APFS (Apple File System), introduced in 2017.
A user's home directory on macOS is /Users/<username>.
Application bundles on macOS are directories ending in .app stored in /Applications.
User-specific preferences on macOS are stored as .plist files in ~/Library/Preferences.
System-wide launch daemons on macOS live in /Library/LaunchDaemons.
Per-user launch agents on macOS live in ~/Library/LaunchAgents.
The macOS system font directory is /System/Library/Fonts; user fonts go in ~/Library/Fonts.
Trash on macOS is stored per volume in a hidden .Trashes directory and in ~/.Trash.
macOS hides the ~/Library folder in Finder by default.
Extended file attributes on macOS include com.apple.quarantine, set on downloaded files by Gatekeeper.
The default shell on macOS since Catalina (10.15) is zsh; earlier it was bash.
The macOS package manager command 'brew' refers to Homebrew, a third-party tool.
The 'defaults' command reads and writes macOS user preference (.plist) values.
The 'launchctl' command manages launchd services on macOS.
The 'diskutil' command manages disks and volumes on macOS.
The 'codesign' command signs and verifies code signatures on macOS.
The 'spctl' command manages the Gatekeeper security assessment policy on macOS.
The 'pmset' command configures power management settings on macOS.
The 'sw_vers' command prints the macOS product name, version, and build.
The 'system_profiler' command reports detailed hardware and software information on macOS.
The 'plutil' command validates and converts property list (.plist) files on macOS.
The 'xattr' command views and edits extended attributes, including removing the quarantine flag.
The 'osascript' command runs AppleScript and JavaScript for Automation from the command line.
The 'sips' command performs scriptable image processing on macOS.
The 'caffeinate' command prevents macOS from sleeping while a command runs.
The 'mdfind' command queries the Spotlight index from the command line on macOS.
The 'security' command manages the macOS Keychain from the command line.
The 'softwareupdate' command installs macOS system updates from the command line.
System Integrity Protection (SIP) on macOS restricts modification of protected system files even by root.
Gatekeeper on macOS blocks running unsigned or unnotarized applications by default.
TCC (Transparency, Consent, and Control) governs app access to files, camera, microphone, and more on macOS.
FileVault provides full-disk encryption on macOS.
The macOS Keychain stores passwords, keys, and certificates in encrypted .keychain-db files.
The macOS Recovery partition is reached by holding Command-R at startup on Intel Macs.
On a Mac keyboard, the Command (Cmd) key is the primary modifier for shortcuts.
Copy, paste, and cut on macOS use Command-C, Command-V, and Command-X.
Spotlight search on macOS is opened with Command-Space.
Force Quit on macOS is opened with Command-Option-Escape.
A screenshot of the whole screen on macOS is taken with Command-Shift-3.
The macOS clipboard manager service is called the pasteboard, accessed via 'pbcopy' and 'pbpaste'.
Windows 11 was released in 2021; its first stable build was 22000.
Windows 10 was released in 2015 and its version numbering used strings like 22H2.
Windows 11 requires UEFI, Secure Boot, and a TPM 2.0 module.
Windows NT is the kernel family underlying all modern Windows versions.
64-bit Windows runs on the x86-64 (AMD64) and ARM64 architectures.
The Windows system directory is C:\Windows\System32 (64-bit binaries on 64-bit Windows).
On 64-bit Windows, 32-bit system binaries are stored in C:\Windows\SysWOW64.
The Windows Registry root HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (HKLM) stores machine-wide settings.
The Windows Registry root HKEY_CURRENT_USER (HKCU) stores settings for the logged-in user.
The Windows Registry root HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT (HKCR) stores file associations and COM class registrations.
The Windows Registry root HKEY_USERS (HKU) contains loaded user profiles by SID.
The Windows Registry root HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG (HKCC) stores the current hardware profile.
The HKLM hive is backed by files in C:\Windows\System32\config (SYSTEM, SOFTWARE, SAM, SECURITY).
Each user's HKCU registry hive is stored in the file NTUSER.DAT in their profile folder.
Programs listed under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run start at user logon.
The key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run holds per-user startup programs.
Installed-program metadata is under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall.
The Windows product name and build are under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion.
Environment variables for the machine are under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Environment.
Windows services are configured under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services.
Common registry value types include REG_SZ (string), REG_DWORD (32-bit number), and REG_BINARY (binary data).
The Windows user profile directory is C:\Users\<username>.
The %APPDATA% environment variable points to C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming.
The %LOCALAPPDATA% environment variable points to C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local.
The %PROGRAMFILES% environment variable points to C:\Program Files by default.
The %TEMP% environment variable points to a per-user temporary files directory.
The %WINDIR% environment variable points to C:\Windows.
Windows uses the backslash (\) as its path separator and drive letters like C:.
Windows path components are case-insensitive but case-preserving.
The Windows Registry Editor is launched with the command 'regedit'.
The 'reg' command queries and edits the Windows Registry from the command line.
The 'powershell' command starts Windows PowerShell; 'pwsh' starts PowerShell 7+.
The 'cmd' command starts the legacy Windows Command Prompt.
The 'sfc /scannow' command checks and repairs protected Windows system files.
The 'DISM' command services Windows images and can repair the component store.
The 'tasklist' and 'taskkill' commands list and terminate processes on Windows.
The 'wmic' command queries Windows Management Instrumentation (deprecated in favor of PowerShell CIM cmdlets).
The 'winget' command is the Windows Package Manager command-line tool.
The 'gpedit.msc' console edits Local Group Policy on Windows Pro editions.
The 'services.msc' console manages Windows services.
The 'msconfig' command opens the System Configuration tool on Windows.
The PowerShell cmdlet Get-ItemProperty reads registry values.
The Windows file 'hosts' is located at C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts.
NTFS is the default file system for Windows system drives.
The FAT32 file system has a maximum single-file size of 4 GB minus 1 byte.
exFAT is a Microsoft file system designed for flash drives without FAT32's 4 GB file-size limit.
Windows drive encryption is provided by BitLocker.
User Account Control (UAC) prompts for elevation before administrative actions on Windows.
Windows Defender is the built-in antivirus and is branded Microsoft Defender.
A Windows SID (Security Identifier) uniquely identifies each user and group account.
Copy, paste, and cut on Windows use Ctrl-C, Ctrl-V, and Ctrl-X.
The Windows Task Manager is opened with Ctrl-Shift-Escape.
Windows line endings are carriage return plus line feed (CRLF, \r\n).
The Linux kernel was first released by Linus Torvalds in 1991.
Linux distributions include Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Arch, and openSUSE.
The 'uname -r' command prints the running Linux kernel version.
Linux commonly runs on x86-64, ARM64 (aarch64), and RISC-V architectures.
The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) defines the standard Linux directory layout.
On Linux, / is the root of the single unified directory tree.
User home directories on Linux are typically under /home/<username>; root's home is /root.
System-wide configuration files on Linux live in /etc.
The /etc/passwd file lists user accounts on Linux.
Encrypted password hashes on Linux are stored in /etc/shadow.
The /etc/fstab file defines file systems to mount at boot on Linux.
The /etc/hosts file maps hostnames to IP addresses on Linux.
User-installed programs commonly live in /usr/local/bin; distro binaries in /usr/bin.
Variable data such as logs and spools lives in /var on Linux; logs are under /var/log.
Temporary files on Linux live in /tmp, which is often cleared on reboot.
The /proc file system on Linux exposes kernel and process information as virtual files.
The /sys file system on Linux exposes kernel device and subsystem information.
Device files on Linux live in /dev, for example /dev/sda for a disk and /dev/null.
Per-user configuration on Linux follows the XDG spec, defaulting to ~/.config.
Boot files and the kernel image on Linux live in /boot.
Debian and Ubuntu use the APT package manager with the 'apt' and 'dpkg' commands.
Fedora and RHEL use the DNF package manager; older versions used YUM; packages are RPMs.
Arch Linux uses the pacman package manager.
openSUSE uses the zypper package manager.
The 'snap' and 'flatpak' commands manage cross-distribution sandboxed application packages.
The 'ls' command lists directory contents on Linux.
The 'chmod' command changes file permission bits on Linux.
The 'chown' command changes file ownership on Linux.
The 'sudo' command runs a command as another user, by default root, on Linux.
The 'ps' command lists running processes on Linux.
The 'grep' command searches text using patterns on Linux.
The 'systemctl' command controls services under the systemd init system.
The 'journalctl' command reads logs from the systemd journal.
The 'mount' command attaches a file system to the directory tree on Linux.
The 'lsblk' command lists block devices on Linux.
The 'ip' command configures network interfaces and routing on Linux (replacing 'ifconfig').
The 'df' command reports file system disk space usage on Linux.
The 'top' and 'htop' commands show live process and resource usage on Linux.
The 'cron' daemon runs scheduled jobs defined in crontab files on Linux.
The 'man' command displays manual pages for Linux commands.
Linux file permissions are read (4), write (2), and execute (1), set for owner, group, and others.
The permission mode 755 means read-write-execute for the owner and read-execute for group and others.
systemd is the most common init system and service manager on modern Linux distributions.
A systemd unit file ending in .service defines how a service is started and managed.
System-wide systemd units live in /etc/systemd/system and /usr/lib/systemd/system.
The Linux superuser account is named root and has user ID 0.
Linux file and directory names are case-sensitive.
Linux uses the forward slash (/) as its path separator.
Linux text files use a single line feed (LF, \n) as the line ending.
A file or directory whose name begins with a dot is hidden by default on Linux.
The most common default shells on Linux are bash and, increasingly, zsh.

The iMac, introduced in August 1998, was the first major product Apple released after Steve Jobs returned as CEO.

The Apple M1 has 68.25 GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.
The Apple M1 Pro chip was released in October 2021 on TSMC's 5-nanometer process, with 33.7 billion transistors.
The Apple M1 Pro has an 8-core (6 performance + 2 efficiency) or 10-core (8 performance + 2 efficiency) CPU.
The Apple M1 Pro has up to a 16-core GPU, supports up to 32GB of unified memory, and provides 200 GB/s of memory bandwidth.
The Apple M1 Max chip was released in October 2021 with a 10-core CPU (8 performance + 2 efficiency) and 57 billion transistors.
The Apple M1 Max has up to a 32-core GPU, supports up to 64GB of unified memory, and provides 400 GB/s of memory bandwidth.
The Apple M1 Ultra chip, released in March 2022, joins two M1 Max dies using Apple's UltraFusion packaging and has 114 billion transistors.
The Apple M1 Ultra has a 20-core CPU (16 performance + 4 efficiency), up to a 64-core GPU, supports up to 128GB of unified memory, and provides 800 GB/s of memory bandwidth.
The Apple M2 chip was released in June 2022 on TSMC's enhanced 5-nanometer (N5P) process, with 20 billion transistors.
The Apple M2 has an 8-core CPU (4 performance + 4 efficiency) and up to a 10-core GPU.
The Apple M2 supports up to 24GB of unified memory with 100 GB/s of memory bandwidth.
The Apple M2's 16-core Neural Engine performs up to 15.8 trillion operations per second.
The Apple M2 Pro chip was released in January 2023 with 40 billion transistors.
The Apple M2 Pro has a 10-core (6 performance + 4 efficiency) or 12-core (8 performance + 4 efficiency) CPU and up to a 19-core GPU.
The Apple M2 Pro supports up to 32GB of unified memory with 200 GB/s of memory bandwidth.
The Apple M2 Max chip was released in January 2023 with a 12-core CPU (8 performance + 4 efficiency) and 67 billion transistors.
The Apple M2 Max has up to a 38-core GPU, supports up to 96GB of unified memory, and provides 400 GB/s of memory bandwidth.
The Apple M2 Ultra chip, released in June 2023, joins two M2 Max dies using UltraFusion packaging and has 134 billion transistors.
The Apple M2 Ultra has a 24-core CPU (16 performance + 8 efficiency), up to a 76-core GPU, supports up to 192GB of unified memory, and provides 800 GB/s of memory bandwidth.
The Apple M3 chip, released in late 2023, was Apple's first chip built on TSMC's 3-nanometer (N3B) process, with 25 billion transistors.
The Apple M3 has an 8-core CPU (4 performance + 4 efficiency) and up to a 10-core GPU.
The Apple M3 GPU introduced Dynamic Caching and hardware-accelerated ray tracing and mesh shading, making it Apple's first GPU with hardware ray tracing.
The Apple M3 supports up to 24GB of unified memory.
The Apple M3 Pro chip, released in November 2023, has an 11-core (5 performance + 6 efficiency) or 12-core (6 performance + 6 efficiency) CPU and 37 billion transistors.
The Apple M3 Pro has up to an 18-core GPU, supports up to 36GB of unified memory, and provides 150 GB/s of memory bandwidth, lower than the M2 Pro's 200 GB/s.
The Apple M3 Max chip, released in November 2023, has a 14-core (10 performance + 4 efficiency) or 16-core (12 performance + 4 efficiency) CPU and 92 billion transistors.
The Apple M3 Max has up to a 40-core GPU, supports up to 128GB of unified memory, and provides up to 400 GB/s of memory bandwidth.
The Apple M3 Ultra chip, released in March 2025, joins two M3 Max dies using UltraFusion packaging and has 184 billion transistors.
The Apple M3 Ultra has up to a 32-core CPU (24 performance + 8 efficiency), up to an 80-core GPU, supports up to 512GB of unified memory, and provides 800 GB/s of memory bandwidth.
The Apple M4 chip debuted in May 2024 in the iPad Pro before reaching Mac models in October 2024, fabricated on TSMC's enhanced 3-nanometer (N3E) process with 28 billion transistors.
The Apple M4's standard CPU configuration has 10 cores (4 performance + 6 efficiency), while its lowest Mac configuration has 9 cores (3 performance + 6 efficiency).
The Apple M4 has up to a 10-core GPU and supports up to 32GB of unified memory.
The Apple M4's 16-core Neural Engine performs up to 38 trillion operations per second.
The Apple M4 Pro chip, released in October 2024, has a 12-core (8 performance + 4 efficiency) or 14-core (10 performance + 4 efficiency) CPU and up to a 20-core GPU.
The Apple M4 Pro supports up to 64GB of unified memory.
The Apple M4 Max chip, released in October 2024, has a 14-core (10 performance + 4 efficiency) or 16-core (12 performance + 4 efficiency) CPU and up to a 40-core GPU.
The Apple M4 Max supports up to 128GB of unified memory.
Apple's UltraFusion packaging connects two Max-series chip dies with a silicon interposer providing up to 2.5 terabytes per second of die-to-die interconnect bandwidth.
Apple announced the Mac's transition from Intel processors to Apple Silicon at WWDC in June 2020.
Apple Silicon Macs use a unified memory architecture (UMA), sharing a single pool of high-bandwidth memory among the CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine.
Rosetta 2 is Apple's binary translation layer that lets Intel x86-64 Mac applications run on Apple Silicon Macs.
The first Apple Silicon Macs, released in November 2020, were the MacBook Air, 13-inch MacBook Pro, and Mac mini, all powered by the M1 chip.
The Mac's transition to Apple Silicon completed in June 2023 when the Mac Pro shipped with the M2 Ultra chip.
The iMac was introduced in August 1998 as the Bondi Blue iMac G3, the first mainstream personal computer to drop the floppy disk drive and standardize on USB.
The iMac was redesigned in April 2021 with the M1 chip and offered in seven colors, its first major redesign since 2012.
The Mac mini was introduced in January 2005 as Apple's first Mac sold without a keyboard, mouse, or display included.
The MacBook Pro was introduced in January 2006, replacing the PowerBook G4 as Apple's first Intel-based professional laptop.
The Mac Pro was introduced in August 2006, replacing the Power Mac G5 as Apple's high-end workstation desktop.
The 2013 Mac Pro redesign was a cylindrical black tower nicknamed the "trash can.".
The Apple Silicon Mac Pro, released in June 2023, uses only the M2 Ultra chip and, unlike prior Intel Mac Pro towers, offers no CPU or GPU upgrade options.
The MacBook Air was introduced in January 2008, unveiled by Steve Jobs pulling it out of a manila envelope.
The MacBook Air moved to Apple Silicon exclusively in November 2020 with the M1 chip.
The 12-inch MacBook (distinct from the Air and Pro) was introduced in 2015 and discontinued in 2019, and had a single USB-C port for both charging and data.
The iMac Pro was introduced in December 2017 in an exclusive Space Gray finish and was discontinued in March 2021.
The Mac Studio was introduced in March 2022 alongside the Studio Display, launching with a choice of M1 Max or M1 Ultra chips.
The redesigned 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro launched in October 2021 with M1 Pro or M1 Max chips, reintroducing HDMI, an SD card slot, and MagSafe charging.
The Apple A4 chip, released in 2010, was Apple's first in-house-designed system-on-chip, debuting in the original iPad and later the iPhone 4.
The original iPhone, released in 2007, used a Samsung-manufactured ARM11-based processor rather than an Apple-designed chip.
The Apple A7 chip, released in 2013 in the iPhone 5s, was the first 64-bit processor shipped in a smartphone.
The Apple A10 Fusion chip, released in 2016 in the iPhone 7, was Apple's first mobile chip with four CPU cores, split between two high-performance and two high-efficiency cores.
The Apple A11 Bionic chip, released in 2017 in the iPhone 8 and iPhone X, introduced Apple's first dedicated Neural Engine for on-device machine learning.
The Apple A12 Bionic chip, released in 2018 in the iPhone XS, was the first smartphone chip manufactured on a 7-nanometer process.
The Apple A14 Bionic chip, released in 2020 in the iPhone 12, was the first Apple chip manufactured on a 5-nanometer process.
The Apple A17 Pro chip, released in 2023 in the iPhone 15 Pro, was the first Apple chip manufactured on a 3-nanometer process.
The first iPad, released in 2010, used the Apple A4 chip and had a 9.7-inch display.
The Apple A4 (2010), a 45-nanometer single-core ARM Cortex-A8-based design, was Apple's first in-house custom system-on-chip and debuted in the original iPad, then the iPhone 4.
The Apple A5 (2011) is a 45-nanometer dual-core ARM Cortex-A9 chip with a PowerVR SGX543MP2 GPU; it debuted in the iPad 2 and then powered the iPhone 4S.
The Apple A5X (2012), used in the third-generation iPad, is a 45-nanometer chip with a quad-core PowerVR SGX543MP4 GPU.
The Apple A6 (2012), used in the iPhone 5, is a 32-nanometer dual-core chip and was Apple's first system-on-chip built around a custom-designed CPU core, codenamed Swift.
The Apple A6X (2012), used in the fourth-generation iPad, is a 32-nanometer chip with a quad-core GPU.

The Apple A7 (2013), used in the iPhone 5S, the iPad Air, and the iPad mini 2, is a 28-nanometer dual-core chip built on Apple's Cyclone microarchitecture and was the first 64-bit ARMv8-A processor shipped in a smartphone.
The Apple A8 (2014), used in the iPhone 6 and 6 Plus, was manufactured by TSMC on a 20-nanometer process, Apple's first chip at that node.
The Apple A8X (2014), used in the iPad Air 2, is a 20-nanometer chip with a triple-core CPU.
The Apple A9 (2015), used in the iPhone 6S, 6S Plus, and the first-generation iPhone SE (2016), was dual-sourced: built by Samsung on a 14-nanometer process and by TSMC on a 16-nanometer process.
The Apple A9X (2015), used in the first-generation 12.9-inch iPad Pro, was manufactured by TSMC on a 16-nanometer process.

The Apple A10 Fusion (2016), used in the iPhone 7 and 7 Plus, was Apple's first quad-core iPhone chip, pairing two high-performance cores with two high-efficiency cores, and was manufactured by TSMC on a 16-nanometer process.
The Apple A10X Fusion (2017), used in the second-generation iPad Pro (10.5-inch and 12.9-inch), was manufactured by TSMC on a 10-nanometer process.
The Apple A11 Bionic (2017), used in the iPhone 8, 8 Plus, and X, is a 10-nanometer six-core chip pairing two high-performance cores with four high-efficiency cores.
The Apple A11 Bionic introduced Apple's first Neural Engine, a dual-core unit rated at 600 billion operations per second.
The Apple A11 Bionic introduced Apple's first in-house-designed GPU, a three-core design, replacing licensed PowerVR/Imagination Technologies graphics.
The Apple A12 Bionic (2018), used in the iPhone XS, XS Max, and XR, was the first 7-nanometer chip shipped in a consumer smartphone, manufactured by TSMC.
The Apple A12 Bionic's second-generation Neural Engine has 8 cores rated at 5 trillion operations per second.
The Apple A12X Bionic (2018), used in the third-generation iPad Pro, is a 7-nanometer chip with an eight-core CPU and a seven-core GPU.

The Apple A12Z Bionic (2020), used in the fourth-generation iPad Pro and in Apple's Developer Transition Kit for the Apple Silicon Mac transition, is functionally identical to the A12X but with an eighth GPU core enabled.
The Apple A13 Bionic (2019), used in the iPhone 11 series and the second-generation iPhone SE (2020), is a six-core chip built on TSMC's second-generation 7-nanometer (N7P) process.
The Apple A14 Bionic (2020), used in the fourth-generation iPad Air and the iPhone 12 series, was the first Apple chip built on a 5-nanometer process, manufactured by TSMC.
The Apple A14 Bionic's fourth-generation Neural Engine has 16 cores rated at 11 trillion operations per second.
The Apple A15 Bionic (2021), used in the iPhone 13 series, the third-generation iPhone SE (2022), and the sixth-generation iPad mini (2021), was manufactured by TSMC on a 5-nanometer process.
The Apple A16 Bionic (2022), used in the iPhone 14 Pro, 14 Pro Max, and later the iPhone 15 and 15 Plus (2023), was the first Apple chip built on a 4-nanometer process, manufactured by TSMC.
The Apple A17 Pro (2023), used in the iPhone 15 Pro and 15 Pro Max, was the first Apple chip built on a 3-nanometer process (TSMC's N3B node).

The Apple A17 Pro introduced hardware-accelerated ray tracing to Apple's GPU architecture and dropped the 'Bionic' branding in favor of 'Pro'; its Neural Engine has 16 cores rated at 35 trillion operations per second.
The Apple A18 (2024), used in the iPhone 16 and 16 Plus, was manufactured by TSMC on its N3E 3-nanometer-class process.
The Apple A18 Pro (2024), used in the iPhone 16 Pro and 16 Pro Max, was manufactured by TSMC on the N3E 3-nanometer-class process and includes a 16-core Neural Engine.
The original iPhone (2007) went on sale June 29, 2007, more than a year before the App Store existed; the App Store launched in July 2008.
The iPhone 3G (2008) was the first iPhone with GPS and 3G cellular support, and it launched alongside the App Store.
The iPhone 3GS (2009) was the first iPhone to support video recording and voice control.
The iPhone 4 (2010) introduced the Retina display and the front-facing camera used for FaceTime video calling.
The iPhone 4S (2011) introduced Siri, Apple's voice assistant.
The iPhone 5 (2012) introduced the Lightning connector and, at 4 inches, the first taller iPhone screen.
The iPhone 5S (2013) introduced Touch ID, Apple's fingerprint-sensor authentication.
The iPhone 6 and 6 Plus (2014) introduced Apple Pay and enlarged the iPhone screen to 4.7 and 5.5 inches respectively.
The iPhone 6S and 6S Plus (2015) introduced 3D Touch, a pressure-sensitive display feature.
The iPhone 7 and 7 Plus (2016) removed the 3.5mm headphone jack and added IP67 water resistance to the iPhone line.
The iPhone 8 and 8 Plus (2017) introduced Qi wireless charging to the iPhone line.
The iPhone X (2017) introduced Face ID and an OLED Super Retina display, and removed the home button in favor of gesture navigation.
The iPhone XR (2018) introduced the Liquid Retina LCD display.
The iPhone 12 series (2020) was the first iPhone generation with 5G support and introduced the MagSafe magnetic accessory system.
The iPhone 14 series (2022) introduced satellite-based Emergency SOS.
The iPhone 15 series (2023) was the first iPhone generation with a USB-C port, replacing the Lightning connector.
The iPhone 16 series (2024) introduced the dedicated Camera Control button.
The first-generation iPad went on sale April 3, 2010, running the Apple A4 chip.
The iPad 2 (2011) added front- and rear-facing cameras to the iPad line.
The third-generation iPad (2012) introduced the Retina display to the iPad line.
The first-generation iPad mini (2012) introduced the 7.9-inch iPad form factor.
The iPad Air 2 (2014) introduced Touch ID to the iPad line.
The first-generation 12.9-inch iPad Pro (2015) introduced Apple Pencil support and the magnetic Smart Connector.
The second-generation iPad Pro (2017) introduced the 120Hz ProMotion adaptive-refresh display.
The third-generation iPad Pro (2018) introduced Face ID and a USB-C port to the iPad line, replacing the home button and Lightning connector on that model.
The fourth-generation iPad Pro (2020) introduced the LiDAR Scanner.
The fifth-generation iPad Pro (2021) was the first iPad powered by an Apple M-series chip (the M1).
The original Raspberry Pi 1 Model B, released in February 2012, uses a Broadcom BCM2835 SoC with a single-core ARM1176JZF-S processor running at 700 MHz.
The Raspberry Pi 1 Model B shipped with a 26-pin GPIO header, which the Raspberry Pi 1 Model B+ replaced with a 40-pin header in July 2014.
The Raspberry Pi 3 Model B, released in February 2016, has a Broadcom BCM2837 quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 SoC clocked at 1.2 GHz and 1GB of RAM.
The Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, released in June 2019, uses a Broadcom BCM2711 quad-core ARM Cortex-A72 SoC clocked at 1.5 GHz and was sold in 1GB, 2GB, 4GB, and 8GB RAM configurations.
The Raspberry Pi 5, released in October 2023, uses a Broadcom BCM2712 quad-core ARM Cortex-A76 SoC clocked at 2.4 GHz and launched with 4GB or 8GB RAM options.
The Raspberry Pi Zero, released in November 2015, uses the same Broadcom BCM2835 SoC as the original Pi 1 but with its single ARM1176JZF-S core clocked higher at 1 GHz, paired with 512MB of RAM.
The Raspberry Pi Pico, released in January 2021, is built around the RP2040 microcontroller with a dual-core ARM Cortex-M0+ processor at up to 133 MHz, 264KB of SRAM, and 26 multi-function GPIO pins.
The BeagleBone Black, released in April 2013, uses a Texas Instruments AM3358 Sitara ARM Cortex-A8 SoC at 1 GHz, 512MB of DDR3 RAM, and exposes 92 GPIO pins across two 46-pin headers.
The NVIDIA Jetson Nano developer kit, released in March 2019, has a quad-core ARM Cortex-A57 CPU at 1.43 GHz, 4GB of LPDDR4 RAM, and a 128-core Maxwell GPU.
The original Raspberry Pi 1 Model B, released in February 2012, uses a Broadcom BCM2835 SoC with a single-core ARM1176JZF-S CPU clocked at 700 MHz.
Raspberry Pi 1 Model B revision 1.0 shipped with 256MB of RAM, and revision 2.0, released in October 2012, increased this to 512MB.
The Raspberry Pi 1 Model B has a 26-pin GPIO header.
The Raspberry Pi 1 Model A, released in February 2013, uses a Broadcom BCM2835 SoC at 700 MHz with 256MB of RAM and no Ethernet port.
The Raspberry Pi 1 Model A has a 26-pin GPIO header.

The Raspberry Pi 1 Model B+, released in July 2014, uses a Broadcom BCM2835 SoC at 700 MHz with 512MB of RAM and introduced the 40-pin GPIO header used by all subsequent standard-size Raspberry Pi boards.
The Raspberry Pi 1 Model A+, released in November 2014, uses a Broadcom BCM2835 SoC at 700 MHz with 256MB of RAM and a 40-pin GPIO header.
The Raspberry Pi 2 Model B, released in February 2015, originally shipped with a Broadcom BCM2836 SoC and a quad-core ARM Cortex-A7 CPU clocked at 900 MHz.
Raspberry Pi 2 Model B revision 1.2, released in October 2016, replaced the BCM2836 with a Broadcom BCM2837 SoC containing a quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 CPU.
The Raspberry Pi 2 Model B has 1GB of RAM and a 40-pin GPIO header.

The Raspberry Pi 3 Model B, released in February 2016, uses a Broadcom BCM2837 SoC with a quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 CPU clocked at 1.2 GHz, has 1GB of RAM, and was the first Raspberry Pi with built-in WiFi and Bluetooth.
The Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+, released in November 2018, uses a Broadcom BCM2837B0 SoC with a quad-core Cortex-A53 CPU clocked at 1.4 GHz and 512MB of RAM.
The Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+, released in March 2018, uses a Broadcom BCM2837B0 SoC with a quad-core Cortex-A53 CPU clocked at 1.4 GHz and 1GB of RAM.
The Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, released in June 2019, uses a Broadcom BCM2711 SoC with a quad-core ARM Cortex-A72 CPU.
The Raspberry Pi 4 Model B was sold with 1GB, 2GB, 4GB, or 8GB of LPDDR4 RAM options.
The Raspberry Pi 4 Model B was the first Raspberry Pi with USB 3.0 ports and true Gigabit Ethernet.
The Raspberry Pi 4 Model B has a 40-pin GPIO header.
The Raspberry Pi 400, released in November 2020, is a keyboard-integrated computer using a Broadcom BCM2711 SoC clocked at 1.8 GHz with 4GB of RAM.
The Raspberry Pi 5, released in October 2023, uses a Broadcom BCM2712 SoC with a quad-core ARM Cortex-A76 CPU clocked at 2.4 GHz.
The Raspberry Pi 5 launched with 4GB and 8GB LPDDR4X RAM options; 2GB and 16GB options were added later.
The Raspberry Pi 5 includes an onboard RP1 southbridge chip, designed by Raspberry Pi, to handle USB, GPIO, and camera and display I/O.
The Raspberry Pi 5 is the first Raspberry Pi board with a PCIe 2.0 interface for connecting M.2 HATs.
The Raspberry Pi 5 has a 40-pin GPIO header.
The Raspberry Pi Zero, released in November 2015, uses a Broadcom BCM2835 SoC with a single-core ARM11 CPU clocked at 1 GHz and 512MB of RAM.
The Raspberry Pi Zero W, released in February 2017, added WiFi and Bluetooth to the Zero's BCM2835 SoC while keeping the same 1 GHz single-core CPU and 512MB of RAM.
The Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, released in October 2021, uses a Broadcom RP3A0 (BCM2710A1) SoC with a quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 CPU clocked at 1 GHz and 512MB of RAM.
The Raspberry Pi Zero, Zero W, and Zero 2 W all have a 40-pin GPIO footprint, though the pins are unpopulated by default.
The Raspberry Pi Pico, released in January 2021, is built around the RP2040 microcontroller chip designed by Raspberry Pi.
The RP2040 chip has a dual-core ARM Cortex-M0+ CPU that can run up to 133 MHz, 264KB of on-chip SRAM, and no built-in flash memory.
The Raspberry Pi Pico includes 2MB of external QSPI flash memory and 26 multifunction GPIO pins.
The Raspberry Pi Pico W, released in June 2022, added an Infineon CYW43439 wireless chip for WiFi and Bluetooth to the same RP2040 microcontroller used by the Pico.
The Raspberry Pi Pico 2, released in August 2024, is built around the RP2350 microcontroller chip.
The RP2350 chip has dual-core processors that can be configured to run as ARM Cortex-M33 cores or as Hazard3 RISC-V cores, clocked up to 150 MHz, with 520KB of SRAM.
The Raspberry Pi Compute Module 1, released in April 2014, uses the same Broadcom BCM2835 SoC at 700 MHz as the original Raspberry Pi.
The Raspberry Pi Compute Module 3, released in January 2017, uses a Broadcom BCM2837 SoC with a quad-core Cortex-A53 CPU at 1.2 GHz and 1GB of RAM.
The Raspberry Pi Compute Module 3+, released in January 2019, uses a Broadcom BCM2837B0 SoC at 1.2 GHz and offered eMMC storage options of 0, 8, 16, or 32GB.
The Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4, released in October 2020, uses a Broadcom BCM2711 SoC with a quad-core Cortex-A72 CPU at 1.5 GHz and RAM options of 1, 2, 4, or 8GB.
The NVIDIA Jetson Nano developer kit, released in March 2019, uses a Tegra X1 SoC with a quad-core ARM Cortex-A57 CPU clocked at 1.43 GHz.
The NVIDIA Jetson Nano's Tegra X1 SoC includes a 128-core Maxwell-architecture GPU.
The NVIDIA Jetson Nano developer kit has 4GB of LPDDR4 RAM.
The NVIDIA Jetson Nano 2GB, released in October 2020, uses the same Tegra X1 SoC and 128-core Maxwell GPU as the original Jetson Nano but with 2GB of RAM.
The NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano module, released in 2023, has an Ampere-architecture GPU with up to 1024 CUDA cores and 32 Tensor Cores.
The NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano module has a 6-core ARM Cortex-A78AE CPU and either 4GB or 8GB of LPDDR5 RAM.
The top-spec NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX module (16GB) has an 8-core ARM Cortex-A78AE CPU, an Ampere GPU with up to 1024 CUDA cores, and 16GB of LPDDR5 RAM.
The top-spec NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin module, released in 2022, has a 12-core ARM Cortex-A78AE CPU and an Ampere GPU with up to 2048 CUDA cores and 64 Tensor Cores.
The top-spec NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin module offers up to 64GB of LPDDR5 RAM.
The BeagleBone Black, released in 2013, uses a Texas Instruments Sitara AM3358 SoC with a single-core ARM Cortex-A8 CPU clocked at 1 GHz.
The BeagleBone Black has 512MB of DDR3L RAM and 4GB of onboard eMMC storage.
The BeagleBone Black exposes two 46-pin expansion headers (P8 and P9), totaling 92 pins, not all of which are GPIO-capable.
The BeagleBone Black's AM3358 SoC includes two 200 MHz Programmable Real-Time Units (PRUs) for low-latency I/O tasks separate from the main CPU.
The Arduino Uno (Rev3) uses an Atmel/Microchip ATmega328P microcontroller clocked at 16 MHz.
The Arduino Uno (Rev3) has 2KB of SRAM, 32KB of flash memory with 0.5KB reserved for the bootloader, and 1KB of EEPROM.
The Arduino Uno (Rev3) has 14 digital I/O pins, of which 6 support PWM output, and 6 analog input pins.
The Arduino Nano uses the same ATmega328P microcontroller at 16 MHz as the Uno but in a smaller breadboard-friendly form factor.
The Arduino Mega 2560 uses an ATmega2560 microcontroller clocked at 16 MHz with 8KB of SRAM and 256KB of flash memory.
The Arduino Mega 2560 has 54 digital I/O pins, of which 15 support PWM output, 16 analog input pins, and 4 hardware UARTs.
The Arduino Uno R4, released in 2023, replaced the ATmega328P with a Renesas RA4M1 ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller clocked at 48 MHz.
The original ESP32 SoC, released by Espressif in 2016, has a dual-core Xtensa LX6 CPU that can run up to 240 MHz, with 520KB of on-chip SRAM.
The original ESP32 SoC integrates both WiFi (802.11 b/g/n) and Bluetooth Classic plus BLE 4.2 radios.
The ESP32-S2 variant has a single-core Xtensa LX7 CPU running up to 240 MHz with WiFi only and no Bluetooth.
The ESP32-S3 variant has a dual-core Xtensa LX7 CPU running up to 240 MHz with both WiFi and Bluetooth 5 (LE).
The ESP32-C3 variant uses a single-core RISC-V (RV32IMC) CPU running up to 160 MHz with WiFi and Bluetooth 5 (LE).
The BBC micro:bit v1, released in 2016, uses a Nordic Semiconductor nRF51822 SoC with an ARM Cortex-M0 CPU at 16 MHz, 16KB of RAM, and 256KB of flash.
The BBC micro:bit v1 has a 5x5 LED matrix of 25 LEDs, a built-in accelerometer and magnetometer, and Bluetooth Low Energy.
The BBC micro:bit v2, released in October 2020, uses a Nordic Semiconductor nRF52833 SoC with an ARM Cortex-M4 CPU at 64 MHz, 128KB of RAM, and 512KB of flash.
The BBC micro:bit v2 added an onboard microphone and speaker compared to the micro:bit v1.
The ThinkPad laptop line was introduced by IBM in 1992.
IBM sold its personal computer division, including the ThinkPad brand, to Lenovo in 2005.
The ATX motherboard form factor, introduced by Intel in 1995, specifies a maximum board size of 305 by 244 millimeters.
The Mini-ITX motherboard form factor, introduced by VIA Technologies in 2001, specifies a maximum board size of 170 by 170 millimeters.
Intel's NUC (Next Unit of Computing) small-form-factor PC line debuted in 2013.
A standard rack unit (U), used to measure the height of server and equipment racks, equals 1.75 inches (44.45 millimeters).
The Valve Steam Deck, released in 2022, is a handheld gaming PC that runs SteamOS, a Linux-based operating system.
The Framework Laptop, first released in 2021, uses swappable Expansion Card modules to let users customize its ports.
Microsoft's Surface hardware line launched in 2012 with the Surface RT and Surface Pro.
IBM introduced the first ThinkPad, the 700C, in October 1992.
IBM's sale of its personal computer division, including the ThinkPad brand, to Lenovo closed on May 1, 2005.
The original ThinkPad industrial design, inspired by a Japanese bento box, was created by designer Richard Sapper.
The red pointing stick embedded in ThinkPad keyboards is called the TrackPoint.
The IBM ThinkPad 701C, released in 1995, used an expanding butterfly-style keyboard that is held in the permanent design collection of New York's Museum of Modern Art.
The Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon, the brand's flagship ultralight business laptop, debuted in 2012.
Classic ThinkPads are finished in matte black, a design cue carried over from the IBM era.
Many Lenovo ThinkPad laptops are tested against the U.S. military's MIL-STD-810G standard for shock, dust, and temperature durability.
Dell was founded by Michael Dell in 1984.
The Dell XPS product line began in 1993 as a series of high-performance Dell Dimension desktop computers.
The Dell Latitude business laptop line launched in 1994.
The Dell XPS 13, launched in January 2015, introduced Dell's 'InfinityEdge' ultra-thin display bezel.
Dell markets its Latitude line for business and enterprise customers and its XPS line for premium consumer computers.
Hewlett-Packard was founded in 1939 by Bill Hewlett and David Packard in a garage in Palo Alto, California.
HP's acquisition of Compaq, announced in September 2001 as a stock deal valued at roughly $25 billion, completed in May 2002.
HP launched its EliteBook line of business laptops in 2008.
HP's Spectre line is its premium consumer laptop family, including the convertible Spectre x360 models.
Microsoft unveiled its Surface device line at a press event in Los Angeles on June 18, 2012.
The Surface RT, released in October 2012, ran Windows RT on an ARM processor.
The Surface Pro, released in February 2013, uses Microsoft's kickstand-plus-detachable-keyboard 2-in-1 tablet form factor, shared with the original Surface RT.
The Surface Book, released in 2015, was Microsoft's first laptop with a display that detaches from a GPU-equipped keyboard base.
Surface Pro and Surface Laptop displays use a 3:2 aspect ratio rather than the 16:9 ratio common on other Windows laptops.
The Surface Laptop, Microsoft's first traditional clamshell Surface device, released in 2017 initially shipping with Windows 10 S.
Framework Computer, founded by Nirav Patel, released its first modular, repairable Framework Laptop in 2021.
Framework laptops accept swappable 'Expansion Cards' that let users choose and change their own port types.
Framework unveiled the Framework Laptop 16, its first model with a swappable graphics module, in 2023.
Valve released the Steam Deck handheld gaming PC on February 25, 2022.
The Steam Deck runs SteamOS, a Linux distribution built on an Arch Linux base.
The original Steam Deck is powered by a custom AMD APU codenamed 'Van Gogh,' combining Zen 2 CPU cores with RDNA 2 graphics.
The original Steam Deck launched in three storage tiers: 64GB eMMC, 256GB NVMe SSD, and 512GB NVMe SSD.
Valve released the Steam Deck OLED model, featuring a 7.4-inch HDR OLED display, in November 2023.
Alienware was founded in 1996 by Nelson Gonzalez and Alex Aguila.
Dell acquired Alienware in 2006.
Alienware's brand logo is a stylized alien head.
The 2014 Alienware Area-51 desktop introduced Alienware's distinctive triangular, three-point case design.
The ATX motherboard form factor, introduced by Intel in 1995, specifies a board measuring 305 mm x 244 mm (12 in x 9.6 in).
The MicroATX (mATX) form factor, introduced in December 1997, specifies a board measuring 244 mm x 244 mm (9.6 in x 9.6 in).
The Mini-ITX form factor, introduced by VIA Technologies in 2001, specifies a board measuring 170 mm x 170 mm (6.7 in x 6.7 in).
Mini-ITX boards are limited to a single expansion slot because of their compact size.
The E-ATX (Extended ATX) form factor commonly specifies a board measuring 305 mm x 330 mm (12 in x 13 in).
The Flex-ATX form factor, introduced by Intel in 1999, specifies a board measuring 229 mm x 191 mm.
The BTX (Balanced Technology Extended) form factor, introduced by Intel in 2004, specifies a board measuring 325 mm x 267 mm.
The Nano-ITX form factor, introduced by VIA Technologies in 2003, specifies a board measuring 120 mm x 120 mm.
The Pico-ITX form factor, introduced by VIA Technologies in 2007, specifies a board measuring 100 mm x 72 mm.
The Mini-DTX form factor, introduced by AMD in 2007, specifies a board measuring 170 mm x 203 mm.
The Mini-STX form factor, also called '5x5,' was introduced by Intel around 2015 and specifies a board measuring 147 mm x 140 mm.
Intel's original NUC (Next Unit of Computing) mini-PC boards, released in 2013, used a roughly 4 in x 4 in (101.6 mm x 101.6 mm) footprint.
A small form factor (SFF) desktop PC is a general term for a compact case smaller than a standard ATX mid-tower, with no single industry-standardized dimension.
Intel's ATX12V 2.0 specification, released in 2003, expanded the ATX motherboard's main power connector from 20 pins to 24 pins.
A standard server rack unit (U) equals 1.75 inches (44.45 mm) of vertical height.
Standard equipment racks, per the EIA-310 standard, are 19 inches (482.6 mm) wide.

A blade server is a stripped-down modular server that slots into a shared chassis providing shared power, cooling, and networking, with dimensions set by the chassis vendor rather than one industry-wide standard.
Intel's Core processor line is tiered from lowest to highest performance as Core i3, Core i5, Core i7, and Core i9, with Core i9 introduced for desktop in 2017.
Intel Core desktop processors of the 12th, 13th, and 14th generations (Alder Lake, Raptor Lake, and Raptor Lake Refresh) use the LGA1700 socket.
Starting with 10th-generation Intel Core processors, the model number's first two digits denote the generation, e.g. Core i7-12700K is 12th generation.
AMD Ryzen desktop processors use the AM4 socket for the Ryzen 1000 through 5000 series, and the AM5 socket beginning with the Ryzen 7000 series introduced in 2022.

In an AMD Ryzen model number such as Ryzen 5 5600X, the single digit (5) is the performance tier, the four-digit number (5000) is the generation series, and a trailing X denotes a higher factory clock speed.
ARM's Cortex processor line is split into three series: Cortex-A for high-performance application processors, Cortex-R for real-time embedded systems, and Cortex-M for low-power microcontrollers.
NVIDIA's GeForce RTX 20 series, launched in 2018 on the Turing architecture, was the first GeForce line to include dedicated ray-tracing (RT) cores and tensor cores.

NVIDIA's consumer GeForce GPU architectures progressed through the codenames Kepler (2012), Maxwell (2014), Pascal (2016), Turing (2018), Ampere (2020), and Ada Lovelace (2022), in that chronological order.
AMD's Radeon RX graphics cards transitioned from the GCN (Graphics Core Next) architecture to the RDNA architecture starting with the Radeon RX 5000 series in 2019.
Intel's Core-series performance tiers rank, from lowest to highest, Core i3, Core i5, Core i7, and Core i9.
In an Intel Core processor model number such as i7-12700K, the leading one or two digits after the hyphen indicate the processor's generation.
Intel's 1st generation Core processors, codenamed Nehalem and Westmere, launched beginning in 2008.
Intel's 2nd through 5th generation Core processors were codenamed Sandy Bridge (2011), Ivy Bridge (2012), Haswell (2013), and Broadwell (2014), respectively.
Intel's 6th through 9th generation Core processors were codenamed Skylake (2015), Kaby Lake (2016), Coffee Lake (2017), and Coffee Lake Refresh (2018), respectively.
Intel's 10th generation Core processors were codenamed Ice Lake (mobile, launched 2019) and Comet Lake (desktop and mobile, launched 2019-2020).
Intel's 11th generation Core processors were codenamed Tiger Lake (mobile, launched 2020) and Rocket Lake (desktop, launched 2021).
Intel's 12th, 13th, and 14th generation Core processors were codenamed Alder Lake (2021), Raptor Lake (2022), and Raptor Lake Refresh (2023), respectively.
Intel's 12th generation Core processors (Alder Lake) introduced a hybrid architecture combining Performance-cores (P-cores) and Efficient-cores (E-cores) on the same chip.
In late 2023 Intel replaced the "Core i" branding and numbered-generation scheme with "Core Ultra," beginning with the Meteor Lake-based Core Ultra Series 1.
In Intel Core processor suffixes, "K" denotes an unlocked multiplier for overclocking.
In Intel Core processor suffixes, "F" denotes a variant with no integrated graphics.
In Intel Core processor suffixes, "U" denotes an ultra-low-power mobile chip.
In Intel Core processor suffixes, "H" denotes a high-performance mobile chip.
Intel desktop socket LGA 1155 was used for 2nd and 3rd generation Core processors (Sandy Bridge and Ivy Bridge).
Intel desktop socket LGA 1150 was used for 4th and 5th generation Core processors (Haswell and Broadwell).
Intel desktop socket LGA 1151 was used for 6th through 9th generation Core processors (Skylake through Coffee Lake Refresh).
Intel desktop socket LGA 1200 was used for 10th and 11th generation Core processors (Comet Lake and Rocket Lake).
Intel desktop socket LGA 1700 was used for 12th through 14th generation Core processors (Alder Lake through Raptor Lake Refresh).
Intel desktop socket LGA 1851 is used for Core Ultra 200S (Arrow Lake) processors.
"LGA" in Intel socket names stands for Land Grid Array, meaning the contact pins are on the socket rather than on the chip.
AMD's Ryzen performance tiers rank, from lowest to highest, Ryzen 3, Ryzen 5, Ryzen 7, and Ryzen 9.
In an AMD Ryzen model number such as Ryzen 7 5800X, the thousands digit (5 in 5800X) denotes the Ryzen series/generation.
AMD's Ryzen 1000, 2000, and 3000 series desktop processors (2017, 2018, and 2019) were built on the Zen, Zen+, and Zen 2 microarchitectures, respectively.
AMD's Ryzen 5000, 7000, and 9000 series desktop processors (2020, 2022, and 2024) were built on the Zen 3, Zen 4, and Zen 5 microarchitectures, respectively.
In AMD Ryzen model suffixes, "X" denotes a higher-clocked, higher-power variant.
In AMD Ryzen model suffixes, "G" denotes a chip with integrated graphics (an APU).
AMD's AM4 desktop socket, used for Ryzen processors from the original Zen through Zen 3 (2017-2022), is a 1,331-pin pin-grid-array (PGA) socket with the pins on the CPU.
AMD's AM5 desktop socket, introduced in 2022 for Zen 4 (Ryzen 7000) and later processors, is a 1,718-pin land-grid-array (LGA) socket with the pins on the socket rather than the CPU.
AMD Threadripper is AMD's high-end desktop/workstation CPU line, positioned above mainstream Ryzen; it launched in 2017.
AMD Threadripper processors have used socket TR4 (1st and 2nd generation), sTRX4 (3rd generation), and sTR5 (Threadripper 7000 series).
AMD's EPYC server processor generations are codenamed Naples (1st gen, 2017, Zen), Rome (2nd gen, 2019, Zen 2), Milan (3rd gen, 2021, Zen 3), and Genoa (4th gen, 2022, Zen 4).
AMD EPYC processors use socket SP3 (Naples, Rome, and Milan) and socket SP5 (Genoa and Bergamo).
ARM Cortex-A processors are application processors designed to run full operating systems, used in devices such as smartphones, tablets, and PCs.
ARM Cortex-R processors are real-time processors designed for deterministic, low-latency response, used in applications such as automotive systems, modems, and storage controllers.
ARM Cortex-M processors are microcontroller-class processors designed for low-power embedded applications.
ARM's big.LITTLE technology pairs high-performance CPU cores with high-efficiency CPU cores of the same instruction set on a single chip.
ARMv8-A, released in 2011, introduced 64-bit support (AArch64) to the ARM architecture.
x86 is a CISC (complex instruction set computing) architecture, while ARM is a RISC (reduced instruction set computing) architecture.
The x86 instruction set originated with Intel's 8086 processor, released in 1978.
x86-64 (also called AMD64), the 64-bit extension of the x86 instruction set, was designed by AMD and introduced in 2003 with the Opteron processor.

NVIDIA's Tesla (2006-2010) and Fermi (2010) GPU architectures powered the GeForce 8/9/100/200/300 series and the GeForce 400/500 series, respectively; Tesla also debuted CUDA, NVIDIA's parallel-computing platform.
NVIDIA's Kepler (2012) and Maxwell (2014) GPU architectures powered the GeForce 600/700 series and the GeForce 900 series, respectively.
NVIDIA's Pascal architecture (2016) powered the GeForce 10 series, including the GTX 1080.
NVIDIA's Turing architecture (2018) powered the GeForce GTX 16 and RTX 20 series; its RTX 20 series introduced dedicated RT (ray-tracing) cores and Tensor cores to GeForce GPUs.
NVIDIA's Ampere architecture (2020) powered the GeForce RTX 30 series.
NVIDIA's Ada Lovelace architecture (2022) powered the GeForce RTX 40 series.
NVIDIA's Blackwell architecture (2025) powered the GeForce RTX 50 series.
NVIDIA CUDA cores are the general-purpose parallel shader cores used for standard graphics and compute workloads; the term debuted with the GeForce 8800 GTX in 2006.
NVIDIA RT cores are dedicated hardware units that accelerate real-time ray-tracing calculations, first introduced with the Turing architecture in 2018.

NVIDIA Tensor cores are dedicated hardware units that accelerate the matrix-multiplication operations used in AI and deep-learning workloads; they debuted in the datacenter Volta architecture's Tesla V100 (2017) before reaching GeForce with Turing in 2018.
NVIDIA DLSS (Deep Learning Super Sampling) is NVIDIA's AI-based upscaling technology, introduced in 2018 alongside the GeForce RTX 20 series.
In GeForce RTX product naming, the "Ti" suffix denotes an enhanced variant with more enabled cores than the base model of the same number.
In GeForce RTX product naming, the "Super" suffix, introduced with the RTX 20 series in 2019, denotes a mid-generation refresh model.

AMD's GCN (Graphics Core Next) architecture debuted in 2012 with the Radeon HD 7000 series and remained AMD's core GPU architecture through several revisions, ending with the Vega architecture (2017).
AMD's RDNA (Radeon DNA) architecture succeeded GCN and debuted in 2019 with the Radeon RX 5000 series.
AMD's RDNA 2 architecture (2020) powered the Radeon RX 6000 series and was also used in the custom GPUs of the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S consoles.
AMD's RDNA 3 architecture (2022) powered the Radeon RX 7000 series and was AMD's first consumer GPU architecture to use a chiplet design.
AMD's RDNA 4 architecture (2025) powered the Radeon RX 9000 series.
AMD's CDNA architecture is a compute-focused datacenter GPU architecture split off from RDNA, debuting in 2020 with the Instinct MI100 accelerator.
AMD introduced dedicated ray-tracing acceleration hardware, called Ray Accelerators, with the RDNA 2 architecture in 2020.
In AMD Radeon product naming, the "XT" suffix denotes a higher-clocked variant of a given model.
Intel Arc is Intel's discrete GPU brand, launched in 2022.
The first Intel Arc GPU architecture, codenamed Alchemist (Xe-HPG), included models such as the Arc A380, A750, and A770.
Intel Arc GPUs include dedicated Xe Matrix Extensions (XMX) engines for AI acceleration, comparable in purpose to NVIDIA's Tensor cores.
Intel's XeSS (Xe Super Sampling) is Intel's AI-based upscaling technology, introduced in 2022 alongside Arc Alchemist.
The second Intel Arc GPU architecture, codenamed Battlemage, launched in December 2024 with the Arc B580.
USB4, introduced in 2019, has a maximum data transfer rate of 40 gigabits per second.
Thunderbolt 3 has a maximum data transfer rate of 40 gigabits per second.
HDMI 2.1 supports a maximum bandwidth of 48 gigabits per second.
DisplayPort 1.4 supports a maximum link bandwidth of 32.4 gigabits per second.
DDR5 SDRAM has a standard operating voltage of 1.1 volts.
SATA III (SATA revision 3.0) has a maximum interface transfer rate of 6 gigabits per second.
SD Card Speed Class 10 guarantees a minimum sustained write speed of 10 megabytes per second.
Bluetooth 5.0 introduced an LE 2M PHY with a raw over-the-air data rate of 2 megabits per second, double the 1 megabit per second rate of the original LE 1M PHY.
PCI Express 4.0 has a per-lane signaling rate of 16 gigatransfers per second, double that of PCI Express 3.0.
USB 1.0, released in 1996, provides a Low Speed data rate of 1.5 Mbit/s.
USB 1.1, released in 1998, provides a Full Speed data rate of 12 Mbit/s.
USB 2.0, released in 2000, provides a High Speed data rate of 480 Mbit/s.
USB 3.0, also branded USB 3.1 Gen 1 and USB 3.2 Gen 1x1, released in 2008, provides a SuperSpeed data rate of 5 Gbit/s.
USB 3.1 Gen 2, also branded USB 3.2 Gen 2x1, released in 2013, provides a SuperSpeed+ data rate of 10 Gbit/s.
USB 3.2 Gen 2x2, released in 2017, provides a data rate of 20 Gbit/s over two lanes of a USB-C connector.
USB4, released in 2019, is based on the Thunderbolt 3 protocol and supports data rates up to 40 Gbit/s.
USB4 Version 2.0, released in 2022, supports data rates up to 80 Gbit/s.
The USB-C connector, released in 2014, is reversible and has 24 pins.
USB Type-A and USB Type-B connectors are not reversible.
USB Power Delivery (PD) 3.0 supports charging at up to 100 watts over a USB-C cable.
USB Power Delivery (PD) 3.1 Extended Power Range (EPR) supports charging at up to 240 watts over a USB-C cable.
Thunderbolt 1, released in 2011, provides 10 Gbit/s per channel over a Mini DisplayPort connector.
Thunderbolt 2, released in 2013, provides 20 Gbit/s by bonding two Thunderbolt 1 channels.
Thunderbolt 3, released in 2015, provides 40 Gbit/s over a USB-C connector.
Thunderbolt 4, released in 2020, provides 40 Gbit/s over a USB-C connector and mandates a minimum PCIe data rate of 32 Gbit/s.
Thunderbolt 5, released in 2024, provides 80 Gbit/s bidirectionally, with a Bandwidth Boost mode reaching 120 Gbit/s in one direction.
HDMI 1.4, released in 2009, has a maximum bandwidth of 10.2 Gbit/s and supports 4K resolution at 30 Hz.
HDMI 2.0, released in 2013, has a maximum bandwidth of 18 Gbit/s and supports 4K resolution at 60 Hz.
HDMI 2.1, released in 2017, has a maximum bandwidth of 48 Gbit/s and supports 8K resolution at 60 Hz.
HDMI 2.1 supports 4K resolution at up to 120 Hz.
An HDMI Ultra High Speed cable is certified to carry the full 48 Gbit/s bandwidth of HDMI 2.1.
DisplayPort 1.2, released in 2009, has a maximum total bandwidth of 21.6 Gbit/s using HBR2 signaling at 5.4 Gbit/s per lane across 4 lanes.
DisplayPort 1.4, released in 2016, has a maximum total bandwidth of 32.4 Gbit/s using HBR3 signaling at 8.1 Gbit/s per lane across 4 lanes.
DisplayPort 1.4 introduced support for Display Stream Compression (DSC).
DisplayPort 2.0, released in 2019, has a maximum total bandwidth of 80 Gbit/s using UHBR20 signaling.
DDR2 SDRAM operates at a standard voltage of 1.8 volts.
DDR3 SDRAM operates at a standard voltage of 1.5 volts, or 1.35 volts for the low-voltage DDR3L variant.
DDR4 SDRAM operates at a standard voltage of 1.2 volts.
DDR5 SDRAM operates at a standard voltage of 1.1 volts.
JEDEC DDR2 SDRAM data rates range from 400 to 1066 MT/s.
JEDEC DDR3 SDRAM data rates range from 800 to 2133 MT/s.
JEDEC DDR4 SDRAM data rates range from 1600 to 3200 MT/s.
The first commercial DDR5 SDRAM modules launched in 2021 with a data rate of 4800 MT/s.
SATA I (SATA 1.5Gb/s), released in 2003, has a maximum interface speed of 1.5 Gbit/s, about 150 MB/s.
SATA II (SATA 3Gb/s), released in 2004, has a maximum interface speed of 3 Gbit/s, about 300 MB/s.
SATA III (SATA 6Gb/s), released in 2009, has a maximum interface speed of 6 Gbit/s, about 600 MB/s.
NVMe SSDs typically connect using 4 lanes of PCI Express (PCIe x4).
The M.2 connector form factor supports both NVMe (PCIe) drives and legacy AHCI (SATA) drives.
An M.2 M-key slot supports up to 4 PCIe lanes, while an M.2 B-key slot supports up to 2 PCIe lanes or SATA.
The U.2 (SFF-8639) connector allows 2.5-inch enterprise drives to use up to 4 lanes of PCI Express for NVMe.
SD Speed Class 2 guarantees a minimum sustained write speed of 2 MB/s.
SD Speed Class 4 guarantees a minimum sustained write speed of 4 MB/s.
SD Speed Class 6 guarantees a minimum sustained write speed of 6 MB/s.
SD Speed Class 10 guarantees a minimum sustained write speed of 10 MB/s.
UHS Speed Class 1 (U1) guarantees a minimum sustained write speed of 10 MB/s.
UHS Speed Class 3 (U3) guarantees a minimum sustained write speed of 30 MB/s.
Video Speed Class V6 guarantees a minimum sustained write speed of 6 MB/s.
Video Speed Class V10 guarantees a minimum sustained write speed of 10 MB/s.
Video Speed Class V30 guarantees a minimum sustained write speed of 30 MB/s.
Video Speed Class V60 guarantees a minimum sustained write speed of 60 MB/s.
Video Speed Class V90 guarantees a minimum sustained write speed of 90 MB/s.
SD Application Performance Class A1 guarantees at least 1500 random read IOPS and 500 random write IOPS.
SD Application Performance Class A2 guarantees at least 4000 random read IOPS and 2000 random write IOPS.
The UHS-I bus interface has a maximum theoretical transfer speed of 104 MB/s in SDR104 mode.
The UHS-II bus interface has a maximum theoretical transfer speed of 312 MB/s.
The UHS-III bus interface, added in SD specification 6.0, has a maximum theoretical transfer speed of 624 MB/s.
802.11a, released in 1999, operates in the 5 GHz band with a maximum data rate of 54 Mbit/s.
802.11b, released in 1999, operates in the 2.4 GHz band with a maximum data rate of 11 Mbit/s.
802.11g, released in 2003, operates in the 2.4 GHz band with a maximum data rate of 54 Mbit/s.
802.11n, marketed as Wi-Fi 4, released in 2009, operates in the 2.4 and 5 GHz bands with a maximum data rate of 600 Mbit/s.
802.11ac, marketed as Wi-Fi 5, released in 2013, operates in the 5 GHz band with a maximum theoretical data rate of 6.93 Gbit/s.
802.11ax, marketed as Wi-Fi 6, released in 2019, operates in the 2.4 and 5 GHz bands with a maximum theoretical data rate of 9.6 Gbit/s.
Wi-Fi 6E, released in 2021, extends the Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) standard into the 6 GHz band.
802.11be, marketed as Wi-Fi 7, released in 2024, operates in the 2.4, 5, and 6 GHz bands and supports channel widths up to 320 MHz.
Bluetooth 1.0, released in 1999, has a maximum gross air data rate of 1 Mbit/s.
Bluetooth 2.0 + EDR, released in 2004, added Enhanced Data Rate with a maximum data rate of 3 Mbit/s.
Bluetooth 3.0 + HS, released in 2009, supports data rates up to 24 Mbit/s via a co-located 802.11 link.
Bluetooth 4.0, released in 2010, introduced Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE).
Bluetooth 5.0, released in 2016, doubled Low Energy data throughput to a maximum of 2 Mbit/s.
Bluetooth 5.1, released in 2019, added direction-finding capability using Angle of Arrival (AoA) and Angle of Departure (AoD).
Bluetooth 5.3, released in 2021, added Connection Subrating to reduce latency and power consumption.
Bluetooth 5.4, released in 2023, added Periodic Advertising with Responses (PAwR).
PCI Express 1.0, released in 2003, transfers at 2.5 GT/s per lane, about 250 MB/s per lane per direction.
PCI Express 2.0, released in 2007, transfers at 5 GT/s per lane, about 500 MB/s per lane per direction.
PCI Express 3.0, released in 2010, transfers at 8 GT/s per lane using 128b/130b encoding, about 985 MB/s per lane per direction.
PCI Express 4.0, released in 2017, transfers at 16 GT/s per lane, about 1969 MB/s per lane per direction.
PCI Express 5.0, released in 2019, transfers at 32 GT/s per lane, about 3938 MB/s per lane per direction.
PCI Express 6.0, released in 2022, transfers at 64 GT/s per lane using PAM4 signaling, about 7877 MB/s per lane per direction.
The Sony PlayStation (PS1), released in 1994, uses a 33.8688 MHz MIPS R3000A-based CPU.
The Sony PlayStation 2, released in 2000, uses a 128-bit "Emotion Engine" CPU clocked at 294.912 MHz.
The Sony PlayStation 3, released in 2006, uses a Cell Broadband Engine CPU clocked at 3.2 GHz.
The Sony PlayStation 4, released in 2013, uses an 8-core AMD Jaguar CPU clocked at 1.6 GHz paired with 8 GB of GDDR5 RAM.
The Sony PlayStation 5, released in 2020, uses an 8-core AMD CPU based on the Zen 2 architecture paired with an AMD RDNA 2 GPU.
The Microsoft Xbox 360, released in 2005, uses a triple-core PowerPC CPU codenamed "Xenon" clocked at 3.2 GHz.
The Microsoft Xbox One, released in 2013, uses an 8-core AMD Jaguar CPU clocked at 1.75 GHz.
The Nintendo Switch, released in 2017, uses an NVIDIA Tegra X1 system-on-chip built around ARM Cortex-A57 CPU cores.
The Valve Steam Deck, released in 2022, uses a custom AMD APU codenamed "Van Gogh" combining Zen 2 CPU cores with RDNA 2 graphics.
The Atari 2600, released in 1977, was originally marketed as the Atari Video Computer System (VCS) before being renamed in 1982.
The Atari 2600 uses a MOS Technology 6507 CPU clocked at approximately 1.19 MHz and has only 128 bytes of RAM.
The Nintendo Entertainment System launched in Japan in 1983 as the Famicom and in North America in 1985.
The NES uses a Ricoh 2A03 CPU, a modified MOS 6502 core clocked at approximately 1.79 MHz, with 2KB of onboard RAM.
The Super Nintendo Entertainment System launched in Japan in 1990 and in North America in 1991.
The SNES uses a Ricoh 5A22 CPU based on the 16-bit 65C816 core, clocked at approximately 3.58 MHz, with 128KB of RAM.
The Sega Genesis, known as the Mega Drive outside North America, launched in Japan in 1988 and in North America in 1989.
The Sega Genesis uses a Motorola 68000 CPU clocked at approximately 7.67 MHz as its main processor, with a secondary Zilog Z80 chip for sound and Master System backward compatibility.
The original PlayStation launched in Japan in December 1994 and in North America in September 1995.
The PlayStation (PS1) uses a 32-bit R3000A-based RISC CPU clocked at approximately 33.87 MHz and reads games from CD-ROM discs.
The PlayStation 2 launched in Japan in March 2000 and had sold over 155 million units by the time its production run ended in 2013.
The PlayStation 2's "Emotion Engine" CPU is a 128-bit MIPS-based processor clocked at 294.912 MHz, paired with 32MB of RDRAM.
The PlayStation 3 launched in Japan and North America in November 2006, followed by Europe and Australia in March 2007.
The PlayStation 3 uses the Cell Broadband Engine CPU, jointly developed by Sony, Toshiba, and IBM, clocked at 3.2 GHz.
The PlayStation 3 pairs its CPU with an Nvidia-developed RSX "Reality Synthesizer" GPU and was the first PlayStation to include a Blu-ray Disc drive as standard.
The PlayStation 4 launched in November 2013.
The PlayStation 4 uses a custom AMD APU combining an 8-core Jaguar CPU at 1.6 GHz with an AMD Radeon GCN-based GPU.
The PlayStation 4 has 8GB of GDDR5 RAM shared between its CPU and GPU.
The PlayStation 5 launched in November 2020.
The PlayStation 5 uses a custom AMD APU combining an 8-core Zen 2 CPU at up to 3.5 GHz with an AMD RDNA 2 GPU.
The PlayStation 5 has 16GB of GDDR6 RAM and a custom high-speed NVMe SSD for storage.
The Nintendo 64 launched in Japan in June 1996 and in North America in September 1996.
The Nintendo 64 uses a NEC VR4300 CPU, a 64-bit MIPS-based processor clocked at 93.75 MHz.
The Nintendo 64's graphics and audio processing is handled by the Reality Coprocessor, designed by Silicon Graphics (SGI), and the console primarily used cartridges rather than optical discs.
The Nintendo GameCube launched in Japan and North America in 2001.
The GameCube uses an IBM PowerPC CPU codenamed "Gekko" clocked at 485 MHz.
The GameCube pairs its CPU with an ATI GPU codenamed "Flipper" and reads games from proprietary 8cm mini-DVD-based optical discs holding about 1.5GB.
The Nintendo Wii launched in North America in November 2006 and in Japan in December 2006.
The Wii uses an IBM PowerPC CPU codenamed "Broadway" clocked at 729 MHz, paired with an ATI GPU codenamed "Hollywood.".
The Wii introduced motion-sensing controls via the Wii Remote and is backward compatible with GameCube discs and controllers.
The Nintendo Wii U launched in North America in November 2012.
The Wii U uses an IBM PowerPC-based tri-core CPU codenamed "Espresso" paired with an AMD Radeon-based GPU codenamed "Latte," and was Nintendo's first home console to output in high definition.
The Wii U GamePad controller has a built-in touchscreen that functions as a second screen for gameplay.
The Nintendo Switch launched worldwide in March 2017.
The Nintendo Switch uses a custom Nvidia Tegra X1 system-on-chip with ARM Cortex-A57 CPU cores and a Maxwell-based GPU, and functions as both a docked home console and a handheld.
The original Xbox launched in North America in November 2001.
The Xbox uses a custom Intel Pentium III CPU clocked at 733 MHz.
The Xbox pairs its CPU with an Nvidia NV2A GPU and was the first major console to include a built-in hard drive (8GB) as standard.
The Xbox 360 launched in North America in November 2005.
The Xbox 360 uses an IBM PowerPC-based tri-core CPU codenamed "Xenon" clocked at 3.2 GHz, paired with an ATI GPU codenamed "Xenos.".
The Xbox One launched in November 2013.
The Xbox One uses a custom AMD APU combining an 8-core Jaguar CPU at 1.75 GHz with an AMD Radeon GCN-based GPU.
The Xbox One shipped with 8GB of DDR3 RAM supplemented by 32MB of embedded SRAM (ESRAM).
The Xbox Series X launched in November 2020.
The Xbox Series X uses a custom AMD APU combining an 8-core Zen 2 CPU at up to 3.8 GHz with an AMD RDNA 2 GPU rated at 12 teraflops.
The Xbox Series X has 16GB of GDDR6 RAM and includes a 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray disc drive.
The Xbox Series S launched alongside the Xbox Series X in November 2020 as a smaller, digital-only console with no disc drive and a lower-power RDNA 2 GPU rated at 4 teraflops.
The Sega Dreamcast launched in Japan in November 1998 and in North America in September 1999.
The Dreamcast uses a Hitachi SH-4 CPU clocked at 200 MHz.
The Dreamcast pairs its CPU with a PowerVR2 GPU co-developed by NEC and VideoLogic, and reads games from a proprietary GD-ROM disc format.
The Dreamcast was the first game console to include a built-in modem for online play and was Sega's last home console before it exited the hardware business in 2001.
The original Game Boy launched in Japan in April 1989 and in North America in July 1989.
The Game Boy uses a Sharp LR35902 CPU, a custom 8-bit chip combining Z80 and 8080 features, clocked at approximately 4.19 MHz, with a monochrome display showing four shades of green.
The Game Boy Color, backward compatible with original Game Boy cartridges, launched in 1998.
The Game Boy Advance launched in Japan in March 2001 and in North America in June 2001.
The Game Boy Advance uses a 32-bit ARM7TDMI CPU clocked at 16.78 MHz alongside a secondary Zilog Z80 core for Game Boy and Game Boy Color backward compatibility.
The Nintendo DS launched in North America in November 2004, with dual ARM9 (main) and ARM7 (secondary) processors and dual screens, the lower of which is a touchscreen.
The Nintendo 3DS launched in Japan in February 2011 and in North America in March 2011.
The Nintendo 3DS uses a dual-core ARM11 CPU clocked at approximately 268 MHz and displays autostereoscopic (glasses-free) 3D graphics on its upper screen.
The PlayStation Portable (PSP) launched in Japan in December 2004 and in North America in March 2005.
The PSP uses a MIPS-based "Allegrex" CPU capable of running up to 333 MHz and reads games from proprietary UMD (Universal Media Disc) optical media.
The PlayStation Vita launched in Japan in December 2011 and in North America in February 2012.
The PlayStation Vita uses a quad-core ARM Cortex-A9 CPU and includes both a front OLED touchscreen and a rear touchpad.
The Valve Steam Deck launched in February 2022.
The Steam Deck uses a custom AMD APU, codenamed "Van Gogh," combining Zen 2 CPU cores with RDNA 2 graphics, and runs SteamOS, a Linux-based operating system.
The Samsung Galaxy S22 Ultra, released in 2022, was the first Galaxy S series phone to include a built-in slot for the S Pen stylus.
The Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra, released in 2024, has a frame made of titanium.
The Samsung Galaxy S8, released in 2017, removed the physical home button in favor of Samsung's Infinity Display design.
The Samsung Galaxy S6, released in 2015, was the first Galaxy S phone without a removable battery or a microSD card slot.
The Google Pixel 6, released in 2021, was the first Pixel phone to use Google's own Tensor system-on-chip instead of a Qualcomm Snapdragon processor.
The original Google Pixel, released in 2016, replaced Google's Nexus line as Google's flagship Android phone series.
