A network hub operates at OSI Layer 1 (physical) and repeats every incoming signal out to all other ports, placing all connected devices in a single collision domain.
A network switch operates at OSI Layer 2 (data link) and forwards frames selectively based on destination MAC addresses, giving each port its own collision domain.
A router operates at OSI Layer 3 (network) and forwards packets between separate networks based on their IP addresses.
A wireless access point connects wireless client devices to a wired network, functioning as a Layer 2 bridge between the two media.

Optical fiber transmits data as pulses of light through a glass or plastic core and is immune to electromagnetic interference, unlike copper cabling which carries electrical signals susceptible to such interference.

Single-mode optical fiber has a narrow core about 9 microns in diameter that carries a single light path for long-distance transmission, whereas multi-mode fiber has a wider core carrying multiple light paths over shorter distances.

Auto-MDIX (automatic medium-dependent interface crossover) is a feature that automatically detects and configures an Ethernet port's transmit and receive pairs, eliminating the need for crossover cables.
The 720p HD display resolution is 1280 by 720 pixels, totaling 921,600 pixels in a 16:9 aspect ratio.
The 1080p Full HD (FHD) display resolution is 1920 by 1080 pixels, totaling 2,073,600 pixels in a 16:9 aspect ratio.

In display resolution notation, the 'p' in 1080p stands for progressive scan, where every horizontal line of the image is drawn on each refresh, while the 'i' in 1080i stands for interlaced, where alternating fields of odd and even lines are drawn.
The 1440p resolution, also called QHD or WQHD, is 2560 by 1440 pixels in a 16:9 aspect ratio, containing exactly four times the pixels of 720p.
The 4K UHD display resolution is 3840 by 2160 pixels, totaling 8,294,400 pixels, which is exactly four times the pixel count of 1080p Full HD.
The 8K UHD display resolution is 7680 by 4320 pixels, totaling 33,177,600 pixels, which is sixteen times the pixel count of 1080p and four times that of 4K UHD.
DCI 4K is the digital cinema resolution standard of 4096 by 2160 pixels defined by Digital Cinema Initiatives, wider than the 3840 by 2160 pixel 4K UHD used for consumer television.
DCI 2K is a digital cinema resolution of 2048 by 1080 pixels defined by Digital Cinema Initiatives.
WUXGA is the 1920 by 1200 pixel resolution and WQXGA is the 2560 by 1600 pixel resolution, both in the 16:10 aspect ratio.
The 16:9 aspect ratio, the standard for high-definition television and most computer monitors, has a width-to-height proportion of approximately 1.778 to 1.
The 4:3 aspect ratio, used by traditional standard-definition television and early computer monitors, has a width-to-height proportion of approximately 1.333 to 1.
The 16:10 aspect ratio, common in productivity monitors and laptops, has a width-to-height proportion of exactly 1.6 to 1, providing more vertical space than 16:9.
Ultrawide monitors marketed as 21:9 have an aspect ratio of roughly 2.37 to 1; a common ultrawide resolution is UWQHD at 3440 by 1440 pixels.
Super ultrawide monitors marketed as 32:9 have an aspect ratio of roughly 3.56 to 1, equivalent in width to two 16:9 displays placed side by side.
TN (Twisted Nematic) LCD panels offer the fastest pixel response times and lowest cost but suffer from narrow viewing angles and poorer color reproduction than IPS or VA panels.

IPS (In-Plane Switching) LCD panels provide wide viewing angles of about 178 degrees and accurate, consistent color, but historically have lower contrast ratios than VA panels and can exhibit 'IPS glow' in dark scenes.
VA (Vertical Alignment) LCD panels offer the highest contrast ratios and deepest blacks among LCD types, but have slower pixel response times and narrower viewing angles than IPS panels.

OLED (Organic Light-Emitting Diode) displays are self-emissive, with each pixel producing its own light so black pixels emit none, yielding effectively infinite contrast, wide viewing angles, and fast response times, but they remain susceptible to permanent burn-in from static images.

Mini-LED is a display backlight technology using thousands of very small LEDs grouped into many local dimming zones behind an LCD panel to improve contrast and peak brightness; it is a backlight type rather than a distinct panel technology.

A display's refresh rate, measured in hertz (Hz), is the number of times per second the screen redraws its image, so a 60 Hz display refreshes 60 times per second and a 144 Hz display 144 times per second.
The hertz, the unit of refresh rate and frequency equal to one cycle per second, is named after German physicist Heinrich Hertz.

Display pixel response time, measured in milliseconds, is the time a pixel takes to change from one state to another, commonly quoted as gray-to-gray (GtG); lower response times reduce motion blur and ghosting.
An 8-bit-per-channel display uses 256 shades for each of red, green, and blue, producing 256 cubed, or 16,777,216 (about 16.7 million) total colors.
A 10-bit-per-channel display uses 1024 shades for each of red, green, and blue, producing 1024 cubed, or 1,073,741,824 (about 1.07 billion) total colors.
A 6-bit-per-channel display produces 262,144 colors, and many low-cost panels use 6-bit color combined with Frame Rate Control dithering to approximate 8-bit output.

Frame Rate Control (FRC) is a display dithering technique that rapidly alternates a pixel between two colors across successive frames to simulate intermediate shades, letting a lower-bit-depth panel approximate the color count of a higher-bit-depth one.
High Dynamic Range (HDR) on displays refers to a wider range of luminance between the darkest and brightest values, combined with a wider color gamut, compared with standard dynamic range (SDR).

HDR10 is an open high dynamic range standard using 10-bit color depth and static metadata applied to an entire piece of content, whereas Dolby Vision supports up to 12-bit color and dynamic metadata that adjusts scene by scene.
Display luminance and brightness are measured in nits, where one nit equals one candela per square meter (cd/m2).
PPI (pixels per inch) measures pixel density on a display, whereas DPI (dots per inch) measures ink dot density in printing; the terms are often used interchangeably but are technically distinct.

The pixel density of a display in PPI is calculated by dividing its diagonal resolution in pixels, found as the square root of the width squared plus the height squared, by the screen's diagonal size in inches.

A display's contrast ratio is the ratio between the luminance of the brightest white and the darkest black it can produce, and OLED achieves effectively infinite contrast because its black pixels emit no light at all.

Screen tearing is a visual artifact in which a horizontal seam appears across the image because the GPU's frame output is not synchronized with the display's refresh cycle, causing parts of two different frames to be shown at once.

VSync (vertical synchronization) prevents screen tearing by forcing the GPU to deliver completed frames in step with the display's refresh rate, but it can introduce input lag and stutter when the frame rate falls below the refresh rate.

Adaptive sync, also called variable refresh rate (VRR), lets a display dynamically match its refresh rate to the GPU's frame output to eliminate tearing without the latency penalty of VSync; implementations include AMD FreeSync, Nvidia G-Sync, and the VESA Adaptive-Sync standard.
SDRAM stands for Synchronous Dynamic Random-Access Memory, meaning its operation is synchronized to the system bus clock so read and write commands are latched on clock edges.
DDR SDRAM stands for Double Data Rate SDRAM, and it transfers data on both the rising and falling edges of the clock signal, doubling data throughput without doubling the clock frequency.
The first-generation DDR SDRAM (DDR1), standardized around 2000, provided data-transfer rates of roughly 200 to 400 mega-transfers per second (DDR-200 through DDR-400).
DDR2 SDRAM, introduced in 2003, provided data-transfer rates of roughly 400 to 1066 mega-transfers per second.
DDR3 SDRAM, introduced in 2007, provided data-transfer rates of roughly 800 to 2133 mega-transfers per second.
DDR5 SDRAM, whose JEDEC specification was published in 2020, defines data-transfer rates beginning at 3200 mega-transfers per second, roughly double DDR4's baseline.
The internal prefetch buffer width of DDR SDRAM is 2n for DDR, 4n for DDR2, 8n for DDR3 and DDR4, and 16n for DDR5, where n is the internal memory bus width.

A rating such as DDR4-3200 denotes an effective data-transfer rate of 3200 mega-transfers per second (MT/s), which corresponds to an actual I/O bus clock of 1600 MHz since DDR transfers data twice per clock cycle.
DIMM stands for Dual In-line Memory Module, a printed circuit board holding DRAM chips with separate electrical contacts on each side of the board.
DDR4 DIMMs have 288 pins.
DDR5 DIMMs also have 288 pins like DDR4, but the key notch is in a different position, making the two generations mechanically and electrically incompatible.
SO-DIMM stands for Small Outline Dual In-line Memory Module, a physically smaller memory module used in laptops, small-form-factor PCs, and some embedded systems.
DDR4 SO-DIMM modules used in laptops have 260 pins, while DDR3 SO-DIMM modules have 204 pins.
DDR5 SO-DIMM modules have 262 pins.

ECC memory (Error-Correcting Code memory) can detect and automatically correct single-bit errors and detect double-bit errors, a scheme known as SEC-DED (single error correction, double error detection).
ECC memory stores 8 extra check bits for every 64 bits of data, giving a 72-bit word width, which physically typically requires one additional DRAM chip per rank compared to non-ECC memory.

A registered (buffered) DIMM, or RDIMM, places a register between the memory controller and the DRAM chips to buffer address and command signals, reducing electrical load and allowing more modules per memory channel; RDIMMs are common in servers.
An unbuffered DIMM, or UDIMM, connects address and command lines directly to the DRAM chips with no intervening register, and is the type typically used in desktop and consumer PCs.
A Load-Reduced DIMM (LRDIMM) buffers the data lines in addition to the address and command lines, further reducing electrical load to enable higher memory capacities in servers.
Dual-channel memory architecture widens the effective bus between the memory controller and memory to 128 bits by operating two 64-bit channels in parallel.
Quad-channel memory architecture operates four 64-bit memory channels in parallel for a combined 256-bit-wide interface, and is common in high-end desktop and server platforms.
A single DDR5 DIMM is internally divided into two independent 32-bit subchannels, in contrast to DDR4 which presents one 64-bit channel per DIMM.

CAS latency (Column Address Strobe latency), abbreviated CL, is the number of clock cycles between the memory controller issuing a read command with a column address and the requested data becoming available on the output.

The true access latency of memory in nanoseconds equals the CAS latency in clock cycles multiplied by 2000 and divided by the data rate in mega-transfers per second, so DDR4-3200 CL16 yields about 10 nanoseconds.
CPU cache is organized into levels, with L1 the smallest and fastest and located closest to the processor core, followed by progressively larger and slower L2 and L3 caches.
An L1 CPU cache is typically on the order of tens of kilobytes per core and is often split into a separate instruction cache (L1i) and data cache (L1d).
An L2 CPU cache is typically hundreds of kilobytes to a few megabytes per core, larger and slower than L1 but faster than L3.
An L3 CPU cache is the largest cache level, ranging from several to tens of megabytes, and is usually shared among all cores of a processor.
CPU caches are built from static RAM (SRAM), which is faster but more expensive and less dense than the dynamic RAM (DRAM) used for main system memory.

Dynamic RAM (DRAM) stores each bit as charge in a tiny capacitor that leaks over time, so its contents must be periodically refreshed, typically about every 64 milliseconds, which is why it is called dynamic.
Static RAM (SRAM) stores each bit in a flip-flop of cross-coupled transistors and needs no periodic refresh while powered, which is why it is called static.
Volatile memory, such as DRAM and SRAM, loses all stored data when electrical power is removed, whereas non-volatile memory, such as flash and ROM, retains its data without power.

RAM is volatile, byte-addressable working memory that the CPU accesses directly and that loses its contents on power loss, whereas storage devices like SSDs and hard drives are non-volatile, block-addressed, and retain data without power but are far slower to access.
The Arduino Uno, released in 2010, is a microcontroller board built around the ATmega328P 8-bit microcontroller.
The Arduino Uno operates at 5-volt logic levels for its digital input and output pins.
The Arduino Uno's analog-to-digital converter has 10-bit resolution, producing integer readings from 0 to 1023.
The ATmega328P belongs to the AVR family of 8-bit RISC microcontrollers, originally developed by Atmel.
Atmel, the original developer of the AVR microcontroller family, was acquired by Microchip Technology in 2016.
The ESP8266 is a low-cost Wi-Fi system-on-chip made by Espressif Systems, containing a 32-bit Tensilica processor and 802.11 b/g/n Wi-Fi.
The ESP8266 system-on-chip supports Wi-Fi networking but has no Bluetooth capability.
The ESP32 is a system-on-chip from Espressif Systems that integrates both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth and commonly features a dual-core processor.
The ESP32 and ESP8266 operate at 3.3-volt logic levels, and applying 5 volts to their GPIO pins can damage them.
The original ESP32 system-on-chip includes two built-in 8-bit digital-to-analog converter (DAC) channels.
The analog-to-digital converters built into the ESP32 have 12-bit resolution.
STM32 is a family of 32-bit microcontrollers made by STMicroelectronics based on ARM Cortex-M processor cores.
Teensy is a line of microcontroller development boards made by PJRC; the Teensy 4.0, released in 2019, uses an NXP i.MX RT1062 ARM Cortex-M7 running at 600 MHz.
The BBC micro:bit, launched in 2016, is a pocket-sized educational microcontroller board featuring a 5-by-5 grid of 25 LEDs and two programmable buttons.
A microcontroller integrates a processor, memory, and input/output peripherals onto a single chip, whereas a microprocessor requires external memory and peripheral chips to function.
A single-board computer such as a Raspberry Pi runs a full operating system, while a microcontroller typically executes a single program directly without an operating system.
I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) is a synchronous serial bus that uses two signal wires: SDA for data and SCL for the clock.
I2C was developed by Philips Semiconductors in 1982 and uses a shared bus in which devices are selected by address, most commonly a 7-bit address.
In I2C standard mode the bus operates at data rates up to 100 kilobits per second, with faster defined modes at 400 kilobits per second and higher.
SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) is a full-duplex synchronous bus that typically uses four wires: MOSI, MISO, SCLK, and a slave/chip-select line.
In SPI, each additional peripheral device sharing the bus requires its own separate slave-select (chip-select) line.
SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) was originally developed by Motorola in the mid-1980s.
UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter) serial communication uses two data wires, TX to transmit and RX to receive, and has no separate clock line.
UART communication requires both devices to agree on a baud rate, the signaling rate in bits per second, with 9600 and 115200 being common values.
PWM (pulse-width modulation) approximates an analog output by rapidly switching a digital signal on and off while varying the duty cycle, the fraction of each period the signal is high.
GPIO stands for general-purpose input/output, referring to microcontroller pins that software can configure as either digital inputs or digital outputs.
Connecting a 5-volt logic output directly to a 3.3-volt logic input can damage the receiving device, so a level shifter is used to interface between the two voltage domains.
Flashing firmware onto a microcontroller means writing a compiled program into its non-volatile flash memory, often through a bootloader over a USB or serial connection.

ENIAC, the Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, was publicly unveiled in 1946 and was one of the earliest general-purpose electronic digital computers, using approximately 18,000 vacuum tubes.

ENIAC was built at the University of Pennsylvania's Moore School of Electrical Engineering, principally designed by John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert, and funded by the United States Army for artillery firing-table calculations.
ENIAC weighed about 30 tons, occupied roughly 1,800 square feet, and used decimal rather than binary arithmetic to represent numbers.

The MITS Altair 8800, introduced in 1975 and featured on the cover of Popular Electronics that January, was built around the Intel 8080 microprocessor and is widely credited with launching the personal computer industry.
The Altair 8800 used the S-100 bus, an expansion bus based on 100-pin edge connectors, which became an early industry standard for microcomputers.
Microsoft's first product was a BASIC interpreter for the Altair 8800, known as Altair BASIC, written by Bill Gates and Paul Allen in 1975.
The Apple I, released in 1976, was designed by Steve Wozniak and sold as a bare assembled circuit board without a case, keyboard, or power supply, priced at 666.66 US dollars.
The Apple I used the MOS Technology 6502 microprocessor and included video display circuitry allowing connection to a monitor or television.
The Apple II, introduced in 1977, was based on the MOS Technology 6502 processor and was among the first personal computers to display color graphics.
VisiCalc, the first electronic spreadsheet program, was released in 1979 for the Apple II and became a major driver of that computer's sales to businesses.

The MOS Technology 6502, an 8-bit microprocessor introduced in 1975, powered landmark computers including the Apple I, Apple II, and Commodore PET, and was notable for its low launch price of about 25 US dollars.

The Commodore PET, introduced in 1977, was an all-in-one personal computer combining a MOS 6502 processor, keyboard, monitor, and cassette tape drive in a single case; PET stood for Personal Electronic Transactor.
The Commodore 64, released in 1982, used the MOS Technology 6510 processor and 64 kilobytes of RAM, from which its name is derived.
The Commodore 64 is widely regarded as the best-selling single computer model of all time, with estimated sales of roughly 12.5 to 17 million units.
The Commodore 64's sound was generated by the MOS Technology 6581 SID (Sound Interface Device) chip, a synthesizer-on-a-chip renowned for its music capabilities among 1980s home computers.
The IBM Personal Computer, model number 5150, was released in August 1981 and was built around the Intel 8088 microprocessor running at 4.77 megahertz.
The IBM PC model 5150 shipped with PC-DOS supplied by Microsoft, and its open architecture using off-the-shelf parts enabled a large market of compatible clone computers.
The Intel 8088, used in the original IBM PC, had a 16-bit internal architecture but an 8-bit external data bus, which allowed cheaper support hardware than a full 16-bit design.
The IBM System/360, announced in 1964, was a family of mainframe computers that pioneered the concept of a compatible architecture spanning multiple models with differing performance and price.
The IBM System/360 established the 8-bit byte as a standard unit and used a 32-bit word architecture, conventions that deeply influenced later computer design.

The original Apple Macintosh, introduced on January 24, 1984, used the Motorola 68000 processor and featured a built-in 9-inch monochrome display with a graphical user interface controlled by a mouse.
The original 1984 Apple Macintosh shipped with 128 kilobytes of RAM and a 3.5-inch floppy disk drive, and was introduced with the '1984' television commercial directed by Ridley Scott.
The Motorola 68000, released in 1979, was a 16/32-bit microprocessor that powered the original Apple Macintosh, the Commodore Amiga, and the Atari ST.
The Xerox Alto, developed at Xerox PARC starting in 1973, was a pioneering computer that introduced the graphical user interface, bitmapped display, and mouse-driven interaction to a working machine.
The Xerox Alto was never sold commercially as a product but strongly influenced later systems, including the Apple Lisa and Macintosh, through its graphical user interface concepts.
The TRS-80, released by Tandy Corporation and sold through Radio Shack stores in 1977, used the Zilog Z80 processor and was one of the earliest mass-marketed personal computers.
The Sinclair ZX Spectrum, released in the United Kingdom in 1982, used a Zilog Z80 processor and became one of the best-selling British home computers of the 1980s.
The Osborne 1, released in 1981, is widely considered the first commercially successful portable computer, weighing about 24.5 pounds with a fold-up case and a 5-inch built-in display.
The Osborne 1 ran the CP/M operating system, used the Zilog Z80 processor, and was bundled with a substantial suite of application software as part of its selling price.
The Zilog Z80, introduced in 1976, was an 8-bit microprocessor binary-compatible with the Intel 8080 that became one of the most widely used CPUs in early home computers and embedded systems.
The Intel 8080, introduced in 1974, was an 8-bit microprocessor that powered the Altair 8800 and helped establish the microcomputer market.
The 'Trinity of 1977' refers to three influential personal computers released that year: the Apple II, the Commodore PET, and the Tandy TRS-80.

The Apple II was designed with eight internal expansion slots, an open-architecture feature championed by Steve Wozniak that let third parties add cards and greatly extended the machine's versatility.
The USB Type-A connector is a flat rectangular plug measuring roughly 12 millimeters by 4.5 millimeters that can only be inserted in one orientation.
The USB Type-B connector is a squarish plug historically used on printers, scanners, and other larger peripherals as the upstream (device-end) connection.
The USB Type-C connector is rated for a minimum of 10,000 mating cycles (insertions and removals) in its specification.
The Micro-USB connector was standardized by the USB Implementers Forum in 2007 and became a common charging and data port on mobile phones before USB Type-C.
The Mini-USB connector was introduced around 2000 for portable devices such as cameras and MP3 players and was later largely superseded by Micro-USB.
The original Universal Serial Bus (USB 1.0) specification was released in January 1996.
USB Power Delivery in its Standard Power Range supplies up to 100 watts, achieved at 20 volts and 5 amperes.
A USB Type-C connection without Power Delivery negotiation supplies 5 volts at up to 3 amperes, providing a maximum of 15 watts.
The 3.5 millimeter designation of a headphone jack refers to the outer diameter of the plug's shaft, and a TRS plug has three conductors (tip, ring, sleeve) carrying stereo left, right, and ground.
A 3.5 millimeter TRRS plug has four conductors (tip, ring, ring, sleeve), adding a microphone signal to the stereo audio and ground carried by a TRS plug.
The quarter-inch audio jack, measuring 6.35 millimeters in diameter, is a larger connector than the 3.5 millimeter jack and is common on musical instruments and professional audio equipment.
The ATX main power connector on a computer motherboard has 24 pins and supplies +3.3V, +5V, +12V, -12V, and +5V standby rails; it was expanded from an earlier 20-pin design.
The EPS12V CPU power connector is an 8-pin connector that supplies +12 volts to the processor voltage regulators through four +12V pins and four ground pins.
A 6-pin PCI Express supplementary power connector is rated to deliver up to 75 watts, while an 8-pin PCI Express connector is rated to deliver up to 150 watts.
A PCI Express x16 expansion slot can itself provide up to 75 watts of power to an installed card.
The 12VHPWR connector, a 16-pin design with 12 power pins plus 4 sideband pins introduced with the ATX 3.0 and PCI Express 5.0 standards, is rated to deliver up to 600 watts.
The SATA power connector is a 15-pin flat connector that supplies +3.3V, +5V, and +12V to storage drives.
The 4-pin Molex peripheral power connector supplies +5 volts and +12 volts and was historically used to power hard drives, optical drives, and fans.
The base 80 PLUS certification requires a computer power supply to be at least 80 percent energy-efficient at 20 percent, 50 percent, and 100 percent of its rated load.
The 80 PLUS power-supply efficiency certification tiers, in ascending order of stringency, are 80 PLUS, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, and Titanium.
A very common DC barrel jack size has a 5.5 millimeter outer diameter with a 2.1 millimeter inner pin diameter, and center-positive polarity is the most typical convention.
A lithium-ion battery cell has a nominal voltage of about 3.7 volts and is typically charged to a maximum of 4.2 volts.
Lithium-polymer (LiPo) batteries use the same lithium-ion chemistry and nominal cell voltage of about 3.7 volts as cylindrical lithium-ion cells, differing mainly in using a soft pouch enclosure.
A nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) rechargeable cell has a nominal voltage of 1.2 volts.
An alkaline battery cell has a nominal voltage of 1.5 volts, which is the standard for AA, AAA, C, and D sizes.
A lead-acid battery cell has a nominal voltage of about 2 volts, so a standard 12-volt car battery contains six such cells connected in series.
The CR2032 lithium coin cell has a nominal voltage of 3 volts, and its name encodes its dimensions of 20 millimeters in diameter and 3.2 millimeters thick.
A standard 9-volt (PP3) battery consists of six 1.5-volt cells connected in series inside a single rectangular casing.
A milliampere-hour (mAh) is a unit of electric charge capacity, where 1 mAh equals 3.6 coulombs, describing how much charge a battery can deliver over time.
A watt-hour (Wh) is a unit of energy equal to amp-hours multiplied by voltage, so a battery's energy in watt-hours equals its charge in amp-hours times its nominal voltage.

Battery capacities stated in milliampere-hours are only directly comparable between cells of the same voltage, whereas watt-hours account for voltage and allow comparison across different chemistries.
In a direct-current circuit, electrical power in watts equals voltage in volts multiplied by current in amperes, expressed by the formula P equals V times I.

Voltage, measured in volts, is the electric potential difference that drives current, while current, measured in amperes, is the rate of electric charge flow; a device draws only the current it needs up to a charger's maximum amperage.
In large language models, a token is the atomic unit of text that the model reads and generates; tokens can be whole words, subword fragments, individual characters, or punctuation marks.
A common English rule of thumb is that one token corresponds to roughly 4 characters of text or about 0.75 words, so roughly 100 tokens equal about 75 words.
Tokenization is the process of converting raw text into a sequence of integer token identifiers that a language model can process, and detokenization reverses this to reconstruct text.

Byte-pair encoding (BPE) is a subword tokenization algorithm that starts from individual characters and iteratively merges the most frequently occurring adjacent pair of symbols into a single new symbol.
Byte-pair encoding originated as a data compression technique described by Philip Gage in 1994 and was later adapted for neural machine translation and language model tokenization.
The transformer is a neural network architecture introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need' by Vaswani and colleagues, and it underlies most modern large language models.

Self-attention is a mechanism by which a transformer computes, for each token, a weighted combination of the representations of all tokens in the sequence, letting the model relate distant words to one another.
Scaled dot-product attention computes attention weights as the softmax of query-key dot products divided by the square root of the key dimension, then uses those weights to combine value vectors.
The parameters, or weights, of a language model are the numerical values learned during training that determine how inputs are transformed into outputs, and they remain fixed during inference.
Pretraining is the initial phase in which a language model learns general language patterns from a very large unlabeled text corpus, typically via self-supervised next-token prediction.
Fine-tuning is the process of further training an already pretrained model on a smaller, more specific dataset to adapt it to a particular task or domain.
Instruction tuning is a form of fine-tuning in which a language model is trained on examples of instructions paired with desired responses, improving its ability to follow natural-language commands.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is a training technique that uses human preference comparisons to train a reward model, which then guides reinforcement learning to align a language model's outputs with human preferences.

A context window is the maximum number of tokens a language model can attend to at once, encompassing both the input prompt and the generated output; text beyond this limit cannot be directly processed.
Language models generate text autoregressively, predicting one token at a time and appending each predicted token to the sequence before predicting the next.
Next-token prediction is the core training objective of most language models, in which the model learns to predict the probability distribution of the token that follows a given sequence.
Logits are the raw, unnormalized numerical scores a language model produces for each possible next token before they are converted into probabilities.

The softmax function converts a vector of logits into a probability distribution by exponentiating each value and dividing by the sum of all the exponentiated values, yielding numbers between 0 and 1 that sum to 1.

Temperature is a sampling parameter that scales a language model's logits before the softmax; low temperature makes output more deterministic and focused, while high temperature makes output more random and varied.
A sampling temperature of 0 makes a language model effectively deterministic by always selecting the highest-probability token, equivalent to greedy decoding.
Greedy decoding is a text generation strategy that always selects the single most probable next token at each step, producing deterministic but often repetitive output.
Top-k sampling restricts a language model's next-token choice to the k tokens with the highest probabilities, renormalizes their probabilities, and samples from that reduced set.

Top-p sampling, also called nucleus sampling, selects the smallest set of most-probable tokens whose cumulative probability meets or exceeds a threshold p, then samples from that dynamically sized set.

Because language models sample from a probability distribution over tokens, generation is stochastic, so the same prompt can yield different outputs on different runs unless decoding is made deterministic.

Perplexity is a metric for evaluating language models, defined as the exponential of the average per-token cross-entropy loss; lower perplexity indicates the model assigns higher probability to the observed text.
An embedding is a dense vector of real numbers that represents a token, word, or piece of text in a continuous space, where proximity between vectors reflects semantic or syntactic similarity.

Positional encoding is a technique that injects information about the order of tokens into a transformer, which is otherwise permutation-invariant and would not distinguish token positions on its own.
The original transformer architecture encoded token positions using fixed sinusoidal functions of varying frequencies added to the token embeddings.

Quantization reduces a neural network's memory footprint and computational cost by representing its weights with lower-precision numeric formats, such as 16-bit floating point, 8-bit integers, or 4-bit integers, at the expense of some numerical precision.
A knowledge cutoff is the date after which a language model has no information from its training data, so it cannot reliably know about events or facts that emerged after that point.
A hallucination in a language model is output that is fluent and plausible-sounding but factually incorrect, fabricated, or unsupported by the model's inputs or training data.
In-context learning is the ability of a large language model to perform a new task from instructions or examples provided within its prompt at inference time, without any updating of its weights.
Cross-entropy loss is the standard objective minimized when training language models, penalizing the model in proportion to the negative log probability it assigned to the correct next token.

An AI agent is a system in which a large language model plans and carries out multi-step tasks by repeatedly selecting and invoking external tools in a loop, observing each result before deciding its next action.

An agent loop is the repeating cycle in which a language model decides on an action, executes it through a tool, and observes the outcome, iterating until the task is complete or a stopping condition is reached.

Tool calling, also called function calling, is a capability in which a language model emits structured output, typically JSON conforming to a predefined schema, that names a function and its arguments so external software can execute it.

In tool calling the language model does not execute the function itself; it produces a structured request that surrounding software runs, after which the result is returned to the model as additional context.

The ReAct pattern, short for Reasoning and Acting, is an agent technique in which a language model interleaves natural-language reasoning steps with actions such as tool calls, using the observation from each action to inform subsequent reasoning.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard, introduced by Anthropic in 2024, that defines a common interface for connecting language-model applications to external tools, data sources, and services.
The Model Context Protocol uses a client-server architecture and the JSON-RPC message format, allowing any compliant model application to communicate with any compliant tool or data server.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique in which relevant documents are retrieved from an external knowledge source and inserted into a language model's prompt so its response is grounded in that information rather than only in its trained parameters.
The term Retrieval-Augmented Generation was introduced in a 2020 research paper by Patrick Lewis and colleagues, which combined a neural retriever with a sequence-to-sequence generator.

An embedding is a fixed-length vector of real numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, image, or other data, positioned so that semantically similar items lie close together in the vector space.

The dimensionality of an embedding is the fixed number of components in its vector; higher dimensionality can capture more semantic nuance but increases memory use and computation for similarity search.
Semantic search retrieves results by comparing the embedding vectors of a query and candidate documents, ranking by closeness in vector space rather than by matching literal words.
Keyword search scores documents by the overlap of literal query terms, weighting rarer terms more heavily, in contrast to semantic search which ranks by meaning.

BM25, short for Best Matching 25, is a probabilistic ranking function that extends TF-IDF with term-frequency saturation and document-length normalization, and is widely used in lexical search engines.
Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors and ranges from -1 to 1, where 1 indicates identical direction, 0 indicates orthogonality, and -1 indicates opposite direction.
Cosine similarity depends only on the orientation of two vectors and ignores their magnitude, which makes it common for comparing text embeddings of differing lengths.
Cosine distance is defined as one minus cosine similarity, ranging from 0 for identical-direction vectors to 2 for opposite-direction vectors.

Besides cosine similarity, vector similarity is commonly measured by Euclidean (L2) distance, the straight-line distance between vectors, and by dot product, which reflects both the angle and the magnitudes of the vectors.

A vector database is a system that stores high-dimensional embedding vectors and supports similarity search, typically using approximate nearest neighbor algorithms to locate the closest vectors quickly.
Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search trades exact accuracy for speed, returning vectors that are very likely, but not guaranteed, to be the true closest matches to a query vector.
HNSW, short for Hierarchical Navigable Small World, is a graph-based approximate nearest neighbor algorithm that organizes vectors into layered proximity graphs to enable fast similarity search.
Hybrid search combines lexical keyword ranking with semantic vector ranking, merging their result lists to capture both exact-term matches and meaning-based matches.
Reciprocal Rank Fusion is a method for merging multiple ranked result lists by adding, for each item, a score equal to one divided by a constant plus the item's rank within each list.
Document chunking is the practice of splitting a large document into smaller segments before embedding them, so that retrieval can return focused passages that fit within a model's context window.

Reranking is a second-stage retrieval step in which an initially retrieved set of candidate documents is reordered by a more accurate but more expensive model to improve the relevance of the top results.

A cross-encoder reranker jointly processes a query and a candidate document together to score their relevance, achieving higher accuracy than separate embedding comparison at greater computational cost.
Grounding is the practice of tying a language model's output to specific retrieved source material, often accompanied by citations, so that claims are verifiable and fabrication is reduced.

Prompt injection is an attack in which text placed inside user input, retrieved documents, or tool output attempts to issue instructions to a language model, causing it to ignore its original directives or take unintended actions.

Indirect prompt injection occurs when malicious instructions are embedded in external content that an AI system later retrieves or reads, such as a web page or document, rather than being typed directly by the user.

Because a language model cannot inherently distinguish instructions from data, a core security principle is to treat retrieved content and tool output as untrusted data rather than as trusted commands.
A jailbreak is a prompt crafted to bypass a language model's safety guardrails, inducing it to produce content or take actions its policies are designed to refuse.

Guardrails are controls placed around a language model that filter or constrain its inputs and outputs, for example blocking disallowed content or validating that responses conform to a required format.

The principle of least privilege applied to AI agents holds that each tool an agent can use should be granted only the minimum permissions necessary, limiting the damage from errors or successful attacks.
An idempotent operation produces the same end state whether it is performed once or many times, which allows a failed action to be safely retried without causing duplicate effects.
Human-in-the-loop is a design pattern in which an AI system pauses to obtain explicit human approval before executing high-risk or irreversible actions, such as transferring money or deleting data.
In Git, the three main areas where file states exist are the working tree (the checked-out files), the staging area (also called the index), and the repository or committed history.
In Git, HEAD is a reference that points to the currently checked-out commit, normally by pointing at the tip of the current branch.
The Git command 'git reset --soft' moves the current branch pointer to the specified commit but leaves both the staging area and the working tree unchanged, so the reverted changes remain staged.

The default mode of git reset is --mixed, which moves the branch pointer and resets the staging area to match the target commit while leaving the working tree files unchanged, so the changes appear as unstaged modifications.
The Git command 'git reset --hard' moves the branch pointer and overwrites both the staging area and the working tree to match the target commit, discarding all uncommitted changes.
In Git, git revert creates a new commit that applies the inverse of a specified commit's changes, undoing its effect while preserving the existing commit history.

Git reset undoes changes by moving a branch pointer to a different commit, whereas git revert undoes changes by adding a new commit, making reset a history-altering operation and revert a history-preserving one.
The Git reflog is a local log that records the history of where HEAD and branch references have pointed over time, enabling recovery of commits that are no longer reachable from any branch.
Git reflog entries are stored only in the local repository and are never transferred during fetch, push, or clone operations.
By default, Git expires reachable reflog entries after 90 days and unreachable reflog entries after 30 days, controlled by the gc.reflogExpire and gc.reflogExpireUnreachable configuration settings.

A detached HEAD state in Git occurs when HEAD points directly at a specific commit rather than at a branch, so new commits made in that state belong to no branch and can become unreachable if not otherwise referenced.
A Git merge combines the histories of two branches, typically producing a merge commit that has two parent commits.
A Git rebase reapplies a series of commits onto a new base commit, creating new commits with new hashes and yielding a linear history instead of a merge commit.
A fast-forward merge in Git occurs when the current branch's tip is a direct ancestor of the branch being merged in, so Git simply advances the branch pointer without creating a merge commit.
Passing the --no-ff option to git merge forces creation of a merge commit even in cases where a fast-forward merge would otherwise be possible.
Git stash saves uncommitted changes from the working tree and staging area onto a stack and reverts the working tree to match HEAD, allowing the saved changes to be reapplied later.
A .gitignore file lists patterns for intentionally untracked files that Git should ignore, but it has no effect on files that are already tracked by the repository.
In Git, 'origin' is the conventional default name given to the remote repository that a local repository was cloned from.
The Git command git pull is equivalent to running git fetch followed by git merge, downloading commits from a remote and then integrating them into the current branch.
The Git command git clone copies an entire repository including its full commit history, creates a remote named origin pointing to the source, and checks out the default branch.
A lightweight tag in Git is simply a named reference pointing directly to a commit and stores no additional metadata.
An annotated tag in Git is stored as a full object in the repository database, recording the tagger's name, email, date, and a message, and it can be cryptographically signed.
The Git command git cherry-pick applies the changes introduced by a specific existing commit onto the current branch as a new commit with a new hash.
A Git commit is traditionally identified by a 40-character hexadecimal SHA-1 hash derived from its contents, including its tree, parent commits, author, committer, and commit message.
A Git merge conflict occurs when two branches make different changes to the same region of a file and Git cannot automatically reconcile them, requiring manual resolution.

When Git marks a merge conflict inside a file, it inserts conflict markers using '<<<<<<<' to begin the current branch's version, '=======' to separate the two versions, and '>>>>>>>' to close the incoming branch's version.
The Git command git fetch downloads commits, files, and refs from a remote repository into local remote-tracking references without modifying the working tree or the current branch.
In Git, the git add command copies changes from the working tree into the staging area (index) in preparation for the next commit.
In Git, the git commit command records the current contents of the staging area as a new commit in the repository's history.
A Git commit object stores a reference to a tree object representing the file snapshot, references to zero or more parent commits, and author and committer metadata.
In a Git repository, the initial commit has no parent, an ordinary commit has exactly one parent, and a merge commit has two or more parents.

Because Git rebase produces new commits with new hashes, rebasing commits that have already been published to a shared remote causes the rewritten commits to diverge from the copies other collaborators hold.
In Git, a branch is a movable pointer to a commit that automatically advances to each new commit made on it, whereas a tag is a fixed pointer that does not move as new commits are added.
In regular expressions the dot metacharacter (.) matches any single character except a line terminator such as newline, unless the dotall or single-line flag is enabled.
In regular expressions the caret (^) is a zero-width anchor that matches at the start of the input, and additionally immediately after every newline when the multiline flag is enabled.
In regular expressions the dollar sign ($) is a zero-width anchor that matches at the end of the input, and additionally immediately before every newline when the multiline flag is enabled.
In regular expressions the quantifier * matches the preceding element zero or more times.
In regular expressions the quantifier + matches the preceding element one or more times.
In regular expressions the quantifier ? matches the preceding element zero or one time, making it optional.
In regular expressions the bounded quantifier {n} matches the preceding element exactly n times.
In regular expressions the bounded quantifier {n,} matches the preceding element at least n times with no upper limit.
In regular expressions the bounded quantifier {n,m} matches the preceding element between n and m times inclusive.

By default regular-expression quantifiers are greedy, matching as many repetitions as possible while still permitting the overall pattern to match, and backtracking to give back characters only when necessary.
In regular expressions appending a question mark to a quantifier, as in *?, +?, ??, or {n,m}?, makes it lazy (reluctant) so it matches as few repetitions as possible.

Possessive quantifiers, written by appending a plus sign as in *+, ++, or ?+, match greedily and never surrender characters through backtracking, and are supported in the Perl/PCRE family, Java, and Ruby.
A regular-expression quantifier applies only to the single immediately preceding atom, which may be a literal character, a character class, an escape sequence, or a parenthesized group.
In regular expressions a character class written as [...] matches exactly one character that is any of the characters listed inside the brackets.
In a regular-expression character class, a caret (^) placed as the first character after the opening bracket, as in [^...], negates the class so it matches any single character not listed.
In a regular-expression character class a hyphen between two characters, such as [a-z], denotes an inclusive range of characters by their code point values.
Inside a regular-expression character class most metacharacters such as ., *, +, and ? lose their special meaning and are treated as literal characters.
In regular expressions the shorthand \d matches a single digit character, and in ASCII mode is equivalent to the character class [0-9].
In regular expressions the shorthand \w matches a single word character, and in ASCII mode is equivalent to [A-Za-z0-9_], including the underscore.
In regular expressions the shorthand \s matches a single whitespace character such as space, tab, newline, carriage return, or form feed.
In regular expressions the uppercase shorthand classes \D, \W, and \S each match any character not matched by their lowercase counterparts \d, \w, and \s respectively.

The shorthand character classes \d, \w, and \s originate in Perl-compatible regular expressions and are absent from POSIX basic and extended regex, which instead use bracket expressions such as [[:digit:]].

In regular expressions \b is a zero-width word-boundary assertion that matches at a position between a word character (\w) and a non-word character, including the start or end of the string adjacent to a word character.
In regular expressions \B is a zero-width assertion that matches at any position that is not a word boundary.
Inside a regular-expression character class the escape \b denotes the backspace character (code point U+0008) rather than a word boundary, in the Perl/PCRE and JavaScript families.
In regular expressions the vertical bar (|) is the alternation operator, matching either the pattern to its left or the pattern to its right, and it has the lowest precedence of all regex operators.

In regular expressions parentheses (...) form a capturing group that both groups a subpattern and records the text it matched, with groups numbered from 1 in the left-to-right order of their opening parentheses.
In regular expressions the syntax (?:...) creates a non-capturing group that groups a subpattern for quantifiers or alternation without allocating a capture-group number.
In regular expressions a backreference such as \1 matches the same literal text that was previously captured by the first capturing group, rather than re-applying that group's pattern.
In regular expressions a backslash before a metacharacter, such as \. or \*, escapes it so that it matches that character literally instead of exercising its special meaning.
The regular-expression flag i enables case-insensitive matching, so alphabetic characters match regardless of whether they are uppercase or lowercase.

The regular-expression multiline flag m changes the anchors ^ and $ so they match at the start and end of each line around newline characters, rather than only at the start and end of the entire input.
The regular-expression dotall or single-line flag, written s in most engines, makes the dot metacharacter (.) also match newline characters.

In Ruby's regular-expression engine the m flag means dotall so the dot matches newlines, and the anchors ^ and $ always match at line boundaries regardless of any flag, differing from the Perl/PCRE convention.

The regular-expression global flag g, characteristic of JavaScript, causes operations to find or replace all matches and enables stateful iteration via a lastIndex property rather than stopping at the first match.

The regular-expression extended or free-spacing flag, written x in the Perl/PCRE family, causes unescaped whitespace in the pattern to be ignored and text after an unescaped # to be treated as a comment.
In the Perl/PCRE family, inline modifiers such as (?i) turn a flag on for the remainder of the enclosing group, while the scoped form (?i:...) applies the flag only to the enclosed subpattern.
In the Perl/PCRE family and languages such as Java and Ruby, \A anchors a match to the very start of the string and \z to the very end, and unlike ^ and $ they are unaffected by the multiline flag.
Named capturing groups are written (?<name>...) in Perl, PCRE, .NET, Java, and JavaScript, whereas Python's re module uses the (?P<name>...) syntax.
In SQL, the logical order of query evaluation is FROM, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then ORDER BY, which differs from the written order in which SELECT appears first.
An SQL INNER JOIN returns only the rows where the join condition matches in both tables, excluding unmatched rows from either side.
An SQL LEFT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right table, filling columns from the right table with NULL where no match exists.
An SQL RIGHT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from the right table plus matching rows from the left table, filling columns from the left table with NULL where no match exists.
An SQL FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, matching them where the join condition holds and filling in NULLs on the side that has no matching row.
An SQL CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product of two tables, so a table with m rows crossed with a table with n rows yields m times n rows.
In SQL's three-valued logic, any comparison with NULL using operators such as = or <> evaluates to UNKNOWN rather than TRUE or FALSE.
In SQL, NULL cannot be tested with the equality operator; the predicates IS NULL and IS NOT NULL are required to check whether a value is or is not NULL.
In SQL, a WHERE clause keeps only rows for which its predicate evaluates to TRUE, discarding rows where the predicate is FALSE or UNKNOWN.
A primary key in a relational table is a column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row and cannot contain NULL values, and each table can have at most one primary key.
A foreign key is a column or set of columns in one table that references the primary key or a unique key of another table, enforcing referential integrity between the two tables.
A unique index on a database column enforces that no two rows may share the same value in that column, whereas a non-unique index permits duplicate values.
Database indexes speed up read queries by providing an ordered data structure, commonly a B-tree, that lets the engine locate matching rows without scanning every row in the table.
ACID is an acronym for the four guarantees of a reliable database transaction: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.
Atomicity in database transactions means a transaction is all-or-nothing: either every operation in it takes effect, or none of them does.
Durability in database transactions means that once a transaction is committed, its changes persist even if the system crashes or loses power immediately afterward.
Isolation in database transactions means concurrently executing transactions produce a result as if they had run one after another, hiding each transaction's intermediate state from the others.
The SQL standard defines four transaction isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE, in increasing order of strictness.
A dirty read is a concurrency anomaly in which a transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not yet committed, and it is permitted only at the READ UNCOMMITTED isolation level.

A non-repeatable read is a concurrency anomaly in which a transaction reads the same row twice and gets different values because another committed transaction modified that row in between; the REPEATABLE READ isolation level prevents it.

A phantom read is a concurrency anomaly in which a transaction re-runs a query and finds new rows that satisfy its condition because another transaction inserted them; only the SERIALIZABLE isolation level fully prevents phantom reads in the SQL standard.

In SQL, the WHERE clause filters individual rows before grouping, while the HAVING clause filters groups after GROUP BY aggregation, which is why aggregate functions can appear in HAVING but not typically in WHERE.
In SQL, COUNT(*) counts all rows in a group including those containing NULLs, whereas COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is not NULL.
In SQL, UNION combines the results of two queries and removes duplicate rows, while UNION ALL concatenates the results and keeps all duplicate rows.
DDL (Data Definition Language) comprises SQL statements such as CREATE, ALTER, and DROP that define or modify the structure of database objects.
DML (Data Manipulation Language) comprises SQL statements such as INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and SELECT that operate on the data stored within tables.
Database normalization is the process of organizing tables to reduce data redundancy and improve integrity by decomposing them according to functional dependencies into normal forms.
First normal form (1NF) requires that every column of a table hold only atomic, indivisible values and that there be no repeating groups within a row.
Second normal form (2NF) requires that a table be in first normal form and that every non-key attribute depend on the whole primary key rather than on only part of a composite key.
Third normal form (3NF) requires that a table be in second normal form and that no non-key attribute depend transitively on the primary key through another non-key attribute.
In SQL, a COMMIT statement makes all changes performed within the current transaction permanent and visible to other transactions.
In SQL, a ROLLBACK statement undoes all changes made within the current transaction, restoring the database to the state it had before the transaction began.
In SQL, the GROUP BY clause partitions rows into groups sharing the same values in the specified columns so that aggregate functions such as SUM, AVG, and COUNT compute one result per group.
The READ COMMITTED isolation level guarantees that a transaction only reads data that has been committed, preventing dirty reads but still allowing non-repeatable reads and phantom reads.

The SERIALIZABLE isolation level is the strictest defined by the SQL standard and prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads by making concurrent transactions behave as though executed sequentially.
In SQL, aggregate functions such as SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX ignore NULL values when computing their results.
In SQL, the ORDER BY clause sorts the final result set, operating on the output rows after SELECT has produced them, with LIMIT/OFFSET (or FETCH) applied afterward.
Unix file permissions are divided into three triads that apply, in order, to the file's owner (user), the file's group, and all other users (often called world or other).
In Unix permissions, the 'other' triad applies to any user who is neither the file's owner nor a member of the file's group.
The Unix octal mode 644 grants the owner read and write permission and grants the group and all others read-only permission, displayed as rw-r--r--.
The Unix octal mode 600 grants the owner read and write permission and gives the group and all others no access, displayed as rw-------.
The Unix octal mode 700 grants the owner read, write, and execute permission and gives the group and all others no access, displayed as rwx------.
The Unix octal mode 777 grants read, write, and execute permission to the owner, the group, and all others alike, displayed as rwxrwxrwx.
The Unix chmod command changes a file's permission bits and derives its name from 'change mode'; it accepts either a numeric octal mode or a symbolic specification.
In Unix chmod symbolic notation, the letters u, g, o, and a refer respectively to the user (owner), the group, others, and all three classes combined.
In Unix chmod symbolic notation, the operator + adds the named permissions, - removes them, and = sets the permissions of that class exactly, clearing any bits not listed.
The Unix chmod argument u+x adds execute permission for the file's owner while leaving all other permission bits unchanged.
The Unix chmod argument go-w removes write permission from both the group and the others classes.

On a Unix directory, execute (search) permission grants the right to traverse or enter the directory and to access entries within it by name, independent of the ability to list the directory's contents.
On a Unix directory, read permission grants the ability to list the names of the directory's entries, while execute permission is required to retrieve those entries' attributes or contents.

The Unix umask specifies permission bits to be withheld from newly created files and directories, turning off the corresponding bits from the default creation permissions rather than adding permissions.
A Unix umask of 022 removes write permission for group and others, yielding default permissions of 755 for newly created directories and 644 for newly created files.
Newly created regular files on Unix begin from a base permission of 666 before the umask is applied, because execute permission is never granted to files by default.
Newly created directories on Unix begin from a base permission of 777 before the umask is applied.
The Unix chgrp command changes the group ownership of a file.
In Unix, the three special permission bits are represented by an optional fourth, leading octal digit that combines setuid (4), setgid (2), and the sticky bit (1).
The sticky bit is conventionally set on the Unix /tmp directory so that any user may create files there while being unable to delete or rename files owned by other users.
The 10-character permission string shown by 'ls -l' consists of a leading file-type character followed by three groups of three characters representing the owner, group, and other permissions.

In an 'ls -l' listing, the leading file-type character is '-' for a regular file, 'd' for a directory, 'l' for a symbolic link, 'c' for a character device, 'b' for a block device, 'p' for a named pipe (FIFO), and 's' for a socket.
In an 'ls -l' listing, a set setuid bit appears in the owner triad's execute position as lowercase 's' when owner execute is also set and as uppercase 'S' when it is not.
In an 'ls -l' listing, a set sticky bit appears in the other triad's execute position as lowercase 't' when others execute is also set and as uppercase 'T' when it is not.
A Unix hard link is an additional directory entry pointing to the same inode as an existing file, so every hard link is an equal reference to identical file data and metadata.
A Unix hard link cannot cross filesystem boundaries because inode numbers are only unique within a single filesystem, and hard links to directories are generally disallowed.
A Unix symbolic link (soft link) is a special file that stores a text path referencing another file by name, and it can span different filesystems and point to directories, unlike a hard link.
A Unix file's data is freed only when its inode link count reaches zero and no process still holds the file open, so removing one hard link does not delete the data while other links remain.
A Unix symbolic link becomes dangling or broken when the file it points to is removed or renamed, whereas the data behind a hard link persists as long as any hard link to it exists.
In Unix, a file's permission bits are stored in the file's inode rather than in the directory entry that names it.
On Unix systems, only a file's owner and the superuser (root) may change that file's permission bits.
On Unix systems the superuser (root, user ID 0) bypasses read and write permission checks on files, but executing a file still requires that at least one of its execute permission bits be set.
The maximum value of a signed 32-bit integer is 2,147,483,647, which equals 2^31 minus 1 and is the largest Unix timestamp such an integer can hold.
If Unix time is stored in an unsigned 32-bit integer, its maximum value of 4,294,967,295 seconds corresponds to 2106-02-07 06:28:15 UTC.
Unix time stored in a signed 64-bit integer will not overflow for roughly 292 billion years, far exceeding the current age of the universe.
In JavaScript, the Date object and Date.now() represent time as the number of milliseconds, not seconds, elapsed since the Unix epoch of 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC.
ISO 8601 is an international standard for representing dates and times, first published by the International Organization for Standardization in 1988.
In ISO 8601 the calendar date is written in big-endian order as YYYY-MM-DD, placing the most significant component first so that chronological order matches alphabetical string sorting.
In ISO 8601 and RFC 3339, the suffix Z (called Zulu) denotes Coordinated Universal Time, equivalent to a zero offset of +00:00.
ISO 8601 uses the 24-hour clock and permits the time 24:00 to denote the end of a given day, equivalent to 00:00 of the following day.
ISO 8601 defines a basic format that omits separators (for example 20230405) and an extended format that includes hyphens and colons (for example 2023-04-05).
ISO 8601 ordinal dates are written as YYYY-DDD, where DDD is the day of the year from 001 to 366.
In the ISO 8601 week-date system, dates are written as YYYY-Www-D where weeks begin on Monday and the day number D runs from 1 (Monday) to 7 (Sunday).
In ISO 8601, week 01 of a year is the week containing that year's first Thursday, equivalently the week containing the 4th of January.
RFC 3339, titled 'Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps' and published in 2002, defines a widely used profile of ISO 8601 for timestamps in Internet protocols.
In C and POSIX strftime formatting, %Y is replaced by the year including the century as a decimal number, normally four digits such as 2023.
In strftime formatting, %m is replaced by the month as a zero-padded decimal number from 01 to 12.
In strftime formatting, %d is replaced by the day of the month as a zero-padded decimal number from 01 to 31.
In strftime formatting, %H is replaced by the hour on the 24-hour clock as a zero-padded decimal number from 00 to 23.
In strftime formatting, %M is replaced by the minute as a zero-padded decimal number from 00 to 59.
In POSIX strftime formatting, %S is replaced by the second as a zero-padded decimal number from 00 to 60, where the value 60 accommodates a leap second.
In strftime formatting, %j is replaced by the day of the year as a zero-padded decimal number from 001 to 366.
In strftime formatting, %A is replaced by the locale's full weekday name, such as Monday, while %a gives its abbreviated form.
In strftime formatting, %B is replaced by the locale's full month name, such as January, while %b gives its abbreviated form.
In strftime formatting, %p is replaced by the locale's designation for AM or PM used with the 12-hour clock.
In strftime formatting, %z is replaced by the UTC offset in the form +hhmm or -hhmm, such as +0530.
In the Gregorian calendar, January, March, May, July, August, October, and December have 31 days; April, June, September, and November have 30 days; and February has 28 days, or 29 in a leap year.
In the 12-hour clock, AM abbreviates the Latin ante meridiem meaning 'before midday' and PM abbreviates post meridiem meaning 'after midday'.
Under the common 12-hour clock convention, noon is written as 12:00 PM and midnight as 12:00 AM.
The Gregorian calendar was introduced in October 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII as a reform of the Julian calendar to correct the drift of the calendar year relative to the solar year.
A MIME type, also called a media type, is a two-part identifier written as type/subtype (for example text/html) that declares the nature and format of a document or byte stream.
MIME, standing for Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, was defined for email in RFC 2045 and RFC 2046, and its media type system was later adopted by HTTP.
The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) maintains the official registry of media types and their subtypes.
The ten registered top-level media types are application, audio, example, font, image, message, model, multipart, text, and video.
A plus-sign suffix in a media type subtype, such as the +xml in image/svg+xml or application/atom+xml, indicates the underlying structured syntax used to encode the data, as standardized in RFC 6839.
The media type application/json identifies JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) text and is defined by RFC 8259.
The media type text/csv, defined in RFC 4180, identifies comma-separated values tabular data.
The media type application/xml identifies XML documents and is defined by RFC 7303.
The media type application/octet-stream denotes arbitrary binary data and is the default type assumed for content whose format is unknown.
The media type multipart/form-data, defined in RFC 7578, is used to submit HTML forms that contain files and requires a boundary parameter that delimits the individual parts.
The media type text/plain identifies unformatted plain text, and in a MIME email context it defaults to the US-ASCII character set.
RFC 9239, published in 2022, designates text/javascript as the standard media type for JavaScript source code and marks application/javascript as obsolete.
The media type image/png identifies Portable Network Graphics raster images.
The media type image/jpeg identifies JPEG-compressed raster images.
The media type image/gif identifies Graphics Interchange Format images.
The media type image/svg+xml identifies Scalable Vector Graphics, an XML-based vector image format.
The media type image/webp identifies WebP images, an image format developed by Google.
The media type audio/mpeg is the standard media type used for MP3 audio files.
The media type video/mp4 identifies video in the MP4 (MPEG-4 Part 14) container format.
The media type application/zip identifies ZIP archive files.
The media type application/gzip, registered in RFC 6713, identifies files compressed with the gzip algorithm.
The charset parameter of a Content-Type header, such as charset=UTF-8, specifies the character encoding used to interpret a text body.
In the HTTP Authorization header, the Bearer scheme defined by RFC 6750 transmits an OAuth 2.0 access token in the form 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'.

In the HTTP Authorization header, the Basic scheme defined by RFC 7617 transmits a user name and password as a Base64 encoding of the string 'username:password', which is encoding only and not encryption.
The HTTP Accept request header lists the media types the client is able to understand, enabling the server to perform content negotiation.
The HTTP Accept-Encoding request header lists the content codings the client can decode, with common values including gzip, deflate, and br for Brotli.
The HTTP Content-Encoding header indicates which encodings, such as gzip, have been applied to the message body so the recipient knows how to decode it.
The HTTP Cache-Control header conveys caching directives such as no-cache, no-store, and max-age, where max-age specifies the maximum age in seconds for which a response may be reused.
The HTTP Location response header specifies a URL and is used to redirect a client to a different resource or to indicate the location of a newly created resource.
Per the original DNS specification, a CNAME record cannot coexist with other record types for the same name and cannot be placed at a zone's apex (root).

A DNS SOA (Start of Authority) record appears exactly once at the top of every DNS zone and stores administrative data including the primary name server, the responsible party's email, and a serial number.

A DNS SOA record contains refresh, retry, and expire timers that govern how secondary name servers synchronize a zone, plus a minimum TTL field that sets how long negative (name-does-not-exist) responses may be cached.
Reverse DNS lookups for IPv4 addresses use the in-addr.arpa domain with the address octets written in reverse order, while IPv6 reverse lookups use the ip6.arpa domain.
A DNS record's TTL (Time To Live) is a value expressed in seconds that specifies how long resolvers may cache the record before they must query for it again.
DNS resolution proceeds through a hierarchy from the root name servers to the top-level domain (TLD) name servers and finally to the authoritative name servers for the specific domain.
The DNS root zone is served by 13 logical root server identities, labeled a.root-servers.net through m.root-servers.net.

A recursive DNS resolver performs the full chain of queries on a client's behalf and returns a final answer, whereas an authoritative DNS server holds and returns the original records for the zones it is responsible for.

CIDR notation appends a slash and a prefix length to an IP address to indicate how many leading bits identify the network, so the number of addresses in the block is 2 raised to the power of the remaining bits.
The OSI reference model defines seven layers, from bottom to top: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, and application.
In the OSI model, IP addressing operates at layer 3 (the network layer) while TCP and UDP operate at layer 4 (the transport layer).
The TCP three-way handshake establishes a connection through three segments: the client sends SYN, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client responds with ACK.
TCP is a connection-oriented protocol that provides reliable, ordered delivery, whereas UDP is a connectionless protocol offering best-effort delivery with no guarantee of ordering or delivery.
Network Address Translation (NAT) rewrites source or destination IP addresses in packet headers, commonly allowing many devices with private addresses to share a single public IPv4 address.
MD5 produces a 128-bit hash digest, conventionally written as 32 hexadecimal characters.
SHA-1 produces a 160-bit hash digest, conventionally written as 40 hexadecimal characters.
SHA-256 produces a 256-bit hash digest, conventionally written as 64 hexadecimal characters.
SHA-512 produces a 512-bit hash digest, conventionally written as 128 hexadecimal characters.
MD5 is cryptographically broken: practical collision attacks exist that produce two different inputs with the same MD5 digest, making it unsuitable for security purposes.
SHA-1 is cryptographically broken: in 2017 researchers from Google and CWI Amsterdam demonstrated the first practical SHA-1 collision, named SHAttered.
A cryptographic hash function is deterministic, meaning the same input always produces the same digest output.
A cryptographic hash function is one-way (preimage resistant): given a digest, it is computationally infeasible to recover an input that produces it.
Collision resistance is the property of a cryptographic hash function that it is computationally infeasible to find two distinct inputs that produce the same digest.
A cryptographic hash function maps input of arbitrary length to a fixed-length output digest.
The avalanche effect is a property of good cryptographic hash and cipher functions where changing a single input bit flips roughly half of the output bits.
Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key for both encryption and decryption.
AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) supports key sizes of 128, 192, and 256 bits and operates on a fixed block size of 128 bits.
AES was standardized by the U.S. NIST in 2001 as FIPS 197 and is based on the Rijndael cipher designed by Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen.
In asymmetric (public-key) cryptography, data encrypted with a recipient's public key can only be decrypted with the corresponding private key.
A digital signature is created with a private key and verified with the corresponding public key.
RSA is an asymmetric cryptosystem introduced in 1977 by Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman, whose security rests on the difficulty of factoring the product of two large prime numbers.
RSA keys are commonly 2048 or 4096 bits in length.
Elliptic-curve cryptography achieves security comparable to RSA using much smaller key sizes, because its security relies on the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem.
Diffie-Hellman is a key-exchange protocol that lets two parties establish a shared secret over an insecure channel without transmitting the secret itself.
Encryption is reversible using a key, hashing is a one-way transformation not meant to be reversed, and encoding is reversible without any key and provides no confidentiality.
HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) combines a cryptographic hash function with a secret key to provide message integrity and authentication, and is defined in RFC 2104.
A salt is a unique random value added to a password before hashing so that identical passwords produce different digests and precomputed rainbow tables become ineffective.
A rainbow table is a precomputed lookup table of hash digests used to reverse unsalted password hashes quickly.
bcrypt, scrypt, and Argon2 are deliberately slow, computationally expensive password-hashing functions designed to resist brute-force cracking.
bcrypt is a password-hashing function based on the Blowfish cipher, introduced in 1999 by Niels Provos and David Mazieres, with a configurable cost factor.
scrypt is a memory-hard password-hashing function that requires large amounts of memory to compute, raising the cost of hardware-based brute-force attacks.
Argon2 won the Password Hashing Competition in 2015 and is a memory-hard function with variants Argon2d, Argon2i, and Argon2id.
Base64 encoding increases the size of the data by approximately 33 percent, because it represents every 3 bytes of input as 4 output characters.
A nonce or initialization vector (IV) must be unique for each encryption operation under the same key, and reusing it can catastrophically weaken the encryption.
TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the cryptographic protocol that secures HTTPS connections, and it is the successor to the deprecated SSL protocol.
A digital signature provides both authenticity and integrity, proving the message came from the holder of the private key and was not altered in transit.
SHA-256 and SHA-512 are members of the SHA-2 family of hash functions, which was first published by the U.S. NIST in 2001.
SHA-3, standardized by NIST in 2015 as FIPS 202, is based on the Keccak algorithm and uses a sponge construction that differs fundamentally from the SHA-2 design.
Semantic Versioning expresses a software version as three dot-separated non-negative integers in the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, such as 2.4.1.
Under Semantic Versioning, the MAJOR version number is incremented when incompatible, backward-breaking changes are made to a public API.
Under Semantic Versioning, the MINOR version number is incremented when new functionality is added in a backward-compatible manner.
Under Semantic Versioning, the PATCH version number is incremented for backward-compatible bug fixes that do not add features.
The Semantic Versioning specification, which reached version 2.0.0, was authored by Tom Preston-Werner, a co-founder of GitHub.
In Semantic Versioning, a major version of zero (0.y.z) denotes initial development, during which the public API is considered unstable and anything may change at any time.
In Semantic Versioning, version 1.0.0 by convention defines the first stable public API of a project.
In Semantic Versioning, a pre-release version is denoted by appending a hyphen and dot-separated identifiers after the patch number, such as 1.0.0-alpha.1 or 1.0.0-rc.1.
