In Semantic Versioning, build metadata is denoted by appending a plus sign and dot-separated identifiers, such as 1.0.0+20130313144700, and this metadata is ignored when determining version precedence.
In Semantic Versioning, a pre-release version has lower precedence than its associated normal release, so 1.0.0-alpha precedes 1.0.0.
In Semantic Versioning precedence, the major, minor, and patch numbers are compared numerically from left to right, and the first difference determines order.
In Semantic Versioning, numeric pre-release identifiers are compared numerically and always have lower precedence than non-numeric identifiers, which are compared lexically in ASCII sort order.
Semantic Versioning requires that once a version is released, its contents must not be modified; any change must be issued as a new version.
In npm version ranges, the caret operator allows updates that do not change the left-most non-zero digit, so ^1.2.3 matches versions from 1.2.3 up to but not including 2.0.0.
In npm version ranges, the tilde operator with a specified minor version allows only patch-level changes, so ~1.2.3 matches versions from 1.2.3 up to but not including 1.3.0.
In npm version ranges, because the caret operator pins the left-most non-zero digit, ^0.2.3 matches versions from 0.2.3 up to but not including 0.3.0.
The MIT License is a permissive open-source license that grants broad reuse rights while requiring that the copyright notice and permission notice be preserved in copies of the software.
Permissive open-source licenses such as MIT, BSD, and Apache 2.0 permit incorporating the code into proprietary, closed-source software without an obligation to release the derivative's source code.
The Apache License 2.0, released by the Apache Software Foundation in 2004, is a permissive license that includes an express grant of patent rights from contributors to users.
The Apache License 2.0 contains a patent-retaliation clause that terminates a licensee's patent grant if that licensee initiates patent litigation alleging the software infringes a patent.
The Apache License 2.0 requires that recipients of modified files be given prominent notice that changes were made and that the contents of any NOTICE file be preserved in derivative works.

The BSD 3-Clause License, also called the New or Modified BSD License, adds to the 2-Clause version a non-endorsement clause forbidding use of the copyright holder's name to promote derived products without permission.
The BSD 2-Clause License, also called the Simplified or FreeBSD License, is a permissive license requiring only retention of the copyright notice and disclaimer in source and binary redistributions.
The GNU General Public License is a copyleft license: works derived from GPL-licensed code, when distributed, must themselves be licensed under the GPL and have their source code made available.
The GNU General Public License was written by Richard Stallman and is published by the Free Software Foundation, with version 2 released in 1991 and version 3 released in 2007.

GPL version 3, published in 2007, added provisions addressing tivoization, the practice of building hardware that blocks modified versions of its software from running, and included an explicit patent grant absent from GPL version 2.

The GNU Lesser General Public License (LGPL) is a weak-copyleft license intended for software libraries that permits proprietary programs to link to the library while requiring modifications to the library itself to remain under the LGPL.

The GNU Affero General Public License (AGPL) extends copyleft to network use: its Section 13 requires that users who interact with the software over a network be offered access to the corresponding source code.

The Mozilla Public License is a file-level, weak-copyleft license under which modifications to individual MPL-licensed source files must remain under the MPL, even when those files are combined with proprietary files in a larger work.
CC0 is a Creative Commons public-domain dedication tool through which a rights holder waives copyright and related rights in a work to the fullest extent permitted by law.
SPDX License Identifiers are standardized short strings, such as MIT, Apache-2.0, and GPL-3.0-or-later, maintained on the SPDX License List to unambiguously reference open-source licenses.

The fundamental distinction in open-source licensing is between permissive licenses, which allow proprietary reuse of the code, and copyleft licenses, which require derivative works to be distributed under the same open license.
The Apache License 2.0 is incompatible with GNU GPL version 2 but is compatible with GPL version 3, allowing Apache-2.0 code to be combined into GPLv3 projects.

Copyleft, a term that plays on the word copyright, refers to the practice of using copyright law to require that all modified and extended versions of a program remain free and carry the same license.
In application/x-www-form-urlencoded form data, a literal plus sign is percent-encoded as %2B, because an unencoded plus sign represents a space.
RFC 3986 designates the characters : / ? # [ ] @ ! $ & ' ( ) * + , ; = as reserved characters that carry special meaning in URIs and must be percent-encoded when used literally as data.
RFC 3986 defines the URI unreserved characters as the ASCII letters, digits, hyphen (-), period (.), underscore (_), and tilde (~), which never require percent-encoding.
In a URL, a literal number sign is percent-encoded as %23, because an unencoded # marks the start of the fragment identifier.
In a URL, a literal question mark is percent-encoded as %3F, because an unencoded ? marks the start of the query component.
An HTML character reference begins with an ampersand (&) and, in its well-formed form, ends with a semicolon (;).
In JSON, string values are delimited by double quotation marks, and single-quoted strings are not permitted.

In JSON strings, the defined two-character escape sequences are backslash-quote, backslash-backslash, backslash-slash, backslash-b, backslash-f, backslash-n, backslash-t, and backslash-r, representing double quote, backslash, slash, backspace, form feed, line feed, tab, and carriage return respectively.

In JSON strings, a Unicode character in the Basic Multilingual Plane (U+0000 to U+FFFF) may be escaped as backslash-u followed by exactly four hexadecimal digits; a character beyond the BMP must be written as a UTF-16 surrogate pair of two such escapes.
Standard JSON forbids a trailing comma after the final element of an array or object.
Standard JSON does not permit comments of any kind.
In JSON, object keys (member names) must be double-quoted strings.
In JSON strings, the forward slash may optionally be escaped as backslash-slash, but escaping it is not required.
In JSON strings, control characters in the range U+0000 through U+001F must be escaped rather than included literally.
In POSIX shell, single quotes preserve the literal value of every enclosed character, so no variable expansion or command substitution occurs inside them.
In POSIX shell, a single quote cannot appear inside a single-quoted string, because single quotes provide no escape mechanism.
In POSIX shell, double quotes group the enclosed text as one field while still allowing variable expansion, written as $variable, and command substitution.
In POSIX shell within double quotes, a backslash retains its escaping function only when it precedes one of the characters dollar sign, backtick, double quote, backslash, or a newline.
In POSIX shell, an unquoted backslash escapes the single character that immediately follows it, removing any special meaning that character would otherwise have.
In CSV as defined by RFC 4180, any field containing a comma, a double quote, or a line break must be enclosed in double quotation marks.
In CSV as defined by RFC 4180, a literal double quote inside a quoted field is escaped by doubling it, written as two consecutive double quotes.
In CSV as defined by RFC 4180, records are separated by a carriage return and line feed (CRLF) sequence.
A byte consists of 8 bits and is written as exactly two hexadecimal digits, since each hexadecimal digit encodes 4 bits.
A nibble is a group of 4 bits, which corresponds to exactly one hexadecimal digit and can represent 16 distinct values from 0 to 15.
Binary is the base-2 positional number system, using only the digits 0 and 1.
Octal is the base-8 positional number system, using the digits 0 through 7, and each octal digit represents exactly 3 bits.

Hexadecimal is the base-16 positional number system, using the digits 0 through 9 followed by the letters A through F, where A equals 10, B equals 11, C equals 12, D equals 13, E equals 14, and F equals 15.
An n-bit binary field can represent exactly 2 to the power of n distinct values.
A signed n-bit two's complement integer represents values from negative 2 to the power of (n minus 1) up to 2 to the power of (n minus 1) minus 1.
In two's complement representation, negating a number is done by inverting all of its bits and then adding one.
In two's complement representation, the most significant bit acts as the sign bit, where 0 indicates a non-negative value and 1 indicates a negative value.
An IEEE 754 single-precision floating-point number (float32) occupies 32 bits, divided into 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 stored fraction (mantissa) bits.
An IEEE 754 double-precision floating-point number (float64) occupies 64 bits, divided into 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits, and 52 stored fraction (mantissa) bits.
The exponent in IEEE 754 single-precision uses a bias of 127, while double-precision uses a bias of 1023.
IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic defines special values including positive infinity, negative infinity, and NaN (Not a Number).
Under IEEE 754, a NaN value is never equal to any value including itself, so an equality comparison of a NaN to itself evaluates to false.
IEEE 754 single-precision provides roughly 7 significant decimal digits of precision, while double-precision provides roughly 15 to 16 significant decimal digits.

Binary floating-point formats such as IEEE 754 cannot exactly represent many finite decimal fractions, including 0.1, because those values are non-terminating in base 2, which produces rounding error.
Two raised to the 16th power equals 65,536.
Two raised to the 20th power equals 1,048,576.
Two raised to the 32nd power equals 4,294,967,296.
Two raised to the 64th power equals 18,446,744,073,709,551,616, approximately 1.8 times 10 to the 19th.
Big-endian byte order stores the most significant byte of a multi-byte value at the lowest memory address, meaning the most significant byte comes first.
Little-endian byte order stores the least significant byte of a multi-byte value at the lowest memory address, meaning the least significant byte comes first.
Shifting an integer's bits left by n positions is equivalent to multiplying that integer by 2 to the power of n, in the absence of overflow.
A logical right shift of an unsigned integer by n positions is equivalent to integer division by 2 to the power of n, discarding the remainder.
